# 12-Week Post-MI Cardiac Conditioning Programme
### Client Profile & Governing Parameters

**Client:** Male, 58 years old | **Status:** 6 months post-MI, Phase II cardiac rehab clearance
**Hard limits:** HR ≤ 115 bpm (70% age-predicted max) at all times | No Valsalva manoeuvre | No maximal-effort lifting | RPE ceiling: 13/20 (Borg Scale — "somewhat hard")

---

## Pre-Programme Essentials

Before week one begins, establish the following non-negotiables with your client and their cardiologist.

**Medical liaison checklist:** Confirm current medications (beta-blockers will blunt HR response — if the client is on one, the 115 bpm ceiling may be artificially low; discuss a symptom-based RPE ceiling as the primary guide alongside HR). Obtain a resting ECG trace and resting HR baseline. Confirm there are no contraindications to resistance training beyond those already noted. Keep the cardiologist's emergency contact visible in the gym.

**Monitoring protocol:** The client wears a chest-strap HR monitor every session — not a wrist-based optical sensor, which is insufficiently accurate for this population. You check HR at the end of every working set and every three minutes during cardio. If HR exceeds 115 bpm, the client stops, sits, and you record the context. If HR does not return below 100 bpm within two minutes of rest, follow your emergency action plan.

**Symptom red flags — stop immediately and call emergency services if:** chest pain or pressure, jaw or arm pain, dizziness, syncope, severe dyspnoea, palpitations, or unusual fatigue beyond expected exertion.

**Breathing protocol:** Because Valsalva is prohibited, every resistance exercise uses a continuous breathing pattern — exhale on the effort (concentric phase), inhale on the return (eccentric phase). Cue this verbally on every set for the first four weeks until it is automatic.

**Baseline assessments (Week 0):**
- Resting HR and blood pressure
- 6-Minute Walk Test (distance covered, HR response, RPE)
- Sit-to-stand test (30-second chair stand)
- Grip strength (dynamometer, both hands)
- Basic movement screen: squat pattern, hip hinge, overhead reach, single-leg balance

---

## Programme Architecture

The 12 weeks are divided into three four-week phases, each building on the last.

| Phase | Weeks | Theme | Sessions/Week |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 — Foundation | 1–4 | Movement quality, cardiac tolerance, habit formation | 3 |
| 2 — Development | 5–8 | Progressive load, aerobic capacity, functional strength | 3–4 |
| 3 — Consolidation | 9–12 | Endurance, independence, lifestyle integration | 4 |

Each week contains a mix of **cardiovascular conditioning** and **resistance/functional training** sessions. Sessions are never back-to-back on consecutive days — always at least one rest or active recovery day between gym sessions.

---

---

# PHASE 1 — FOUNDATION (Weeks 1–4)

**Phase goals:** Establish safe HR response to exercise, build movement competency, develop the breathing habit, create a positive psychological relationship with the gym environment post-cardiac event.

**Resistance parameters:** 2–3 sets | 12–15 reps | Load chosen so HR stays ≤ 110 bpm and RPE never exceeds 11–12 ("light to fairly light") | Rest 90 seconds between sets minimum.

**Cardio parameters:** Continuous low-intensity steady state only. Target HR 95–108 bpm. RPE 10–11.

---

### Week 1

**Session structure this week:** Three sessions — two resistance/functional days, one cardio day. Sessions capped at 35 minutes of active work.

---

**Session 1 — Resistance/Functional A**

Begin with a 10-minute warm-up: 5 minutes on the recumbent bike at the lowest resistance, pedalling at a comfortable cadence, followed by 5 minutes of gentle mobility — seated thoracic rotations (10 each side), ankle circles (10 each direction), and standing wall slides (10 reps, arms sliding up a wall to open the chest and shoulders). Check HR before proceeding. It should be below 95 bpm.

*Working sets:*

**Seated leg press** — 2 sets × 15 reps. Use a very light load — this is a movement quality session, not a strength session. Feet hip-width apart, toes slightly out. Exhale as you press, inhale as you return. Do not lock the knees at the top. Rest 90 seconds. Check HR.

**Seated cable row (low pulley, neutral grip)** — 2 sets × 15 reps. Sit tall, retract the shoulder blades before pulling, exhale on the pull, inhale on the return. Light load. Rest 90 seconds.

**Goblet squat to box (box squat)** — 2 sets × 12 reps. Use a light dumbbell (4–6 kg) or no weight at all. The box height should allow the client to sit back comfortably — start with a high box (chair height). This teaches the squat pattern safely. Exhale on the stand, inhale on the sit. Rest 90 seconds.

**Standing dumbbell shoulder press (light)** — 2 sets × 12 reps. Use 3–5 kg. Seated is also acceptable if standing causes any instability. Exhale on the press, inhale on the lower. Do not arch the lower back — cue a gentle abdominal brace (not a breath-hold). Rest 90 seconds.

**Plank (forearm, from knees)** — 2 sets × 20 seconds. Breathe continuously throughout — this is critical. If the client holds their breath at any point, stop the set. Rest 60 seconds between sets.

Cool-down: 5 minutes slow walking on the treadmill at 2.5 km/h, then 5 minutes of seated stretching — hamstrings, hip flexors, chest opener (hands clasped behind back, gentle lift). Final HR check — should be below 90 bpm before the client leaves.

---

**Session 2 — Cardiovascular Conditioning A**

Warm-up: 5 minutes on the recumbent bike, very easy, no resistance.

Main work: 20 minutes on the recumbent bike at a resistance level that keeps HR between 95 and 108 bpm. The client should be able to speak in full sentences throughout. Check HR every 3 minutes and record it. If HR climbs above 108 bpm, reduce resistance immediately. RPE should feel like a 10–11 — "very light to fairly light."

Cool-down: 5 minutes at minimal resistance, then 5 minutes seated rest with HR monitoring.

**Why the recumbent bike in Week 1?** The recumbent position reduces cardiac preload compared to upright cycling and eliminates the balance demands of a treadmill, making it the safest cardiovascular starting point for this population.

---

**Session 3 — Resistance/Functional B**

Warm-up: Same protocol as Session 1.

*Working sets:*

**Leg curl (seated machine)** — 2 sets × 15 reps. Isolates the hamstrings without spinal loading. Light load. Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return. Rest 90 seconds.

**Chest press (machine, not free weight)** — 2 sets × 15 reps. The machine guides the path and eliminates the stabilisation demand of a barbell or heavy dumbbell, keeping effort controlled. Light load. Exhale on the press. Rest 90 seconds.

**Step-up (low step, 10–15 cm)** — 2 sets × 10 reps each leg. Hold a light dumbbell in each hand (2–4 kg) or bodyweight only. Step up, stand tall, step down with control. Exhale on the step up. Rest 90 seconds.

**Lat pulldown (wide grip, to chin level)** — 2 sets × 15 reps. Do not pull behind the neck. Exhale on the pull-down, inhale on the return. Light load. Rest 90 seconds.

**Dead bug (modified)** — 2 sets × 8 reps each side. Client lies on their back, knees bent to 90 degrees, arms pointing to the ceiling. Slowly lower one arm overhead while extending the opposite leg, keeping the lower back pressed gently into the floor. Breathe continuously — exhale as the limbs extend. This is an excellent anti-Valsalva core exercise. Rest 60 seconds.

Cool-down: Same as Session 1.

---

### Week 2

**Progression from Week 1:** Add one set to each exercise (moving from 2 to 3 sets on most exercises). Cardio duration increases by 5 minutes. Load remains the same — do not increase weight until movement quality and HR response are both consistently good.

**Session 1 — Resistance/Functional A (Week 2)**

Warm-up: Same 10-minute protocol.

*Working sets (3 sets × 15 reps unless noted):*

- Seated leg press — 3 × 15. If HR stayed comfortably below 108 bpm last week, you may add a small increment of load (5 kg on the machine stack).
- Seated cable row — 3 × 15. Same load as Week 1 unless HR response allows a small increase.
- Goblet squat to box — 3 × 12. Can progress to a slightly lower box if the client is comfortable.
- Standing dumbbell shoulder press — 3 × 12.
- Plank from knees — 3 × 25 seconds. Continuous breathing mandatory.

Cool-down: Same.

---

**Session 2 — Cardiovascular Conditioning A (Week 2)**

Warm-up: 5 minutes recumbent bike.

- Have a conversation with the client about how they feel — energy levels, sleep, confidence, any symptoms.

# PHASE 2 — DEVELOPMENT (Weeks 5–8)

**Phase goals:** Increase aerobic capacity meaningfully, introduce progressive resistance loading within safe parameters, add a fourth training session per week, and begin functional movement patterns that translate to daily life.

# Cardiac-Health Nutrition Plan
### Integrated with the 12-Week Post-MI Conditioning Programme

---

## Governing Principles

Before presenting specific guidance, it is important to establish the nutritional framework appropriate for this client. A 58-year-old male, six months post-MI, is almost certainly on a combination of medications that interact with diet in clinically meaningful ways. The nutrition plan below is designed to complement — not replace — any dietary advice given by his cardiologist or a registered dietitian. Before implementing this plan, confirm the following with the client and his medical team.

**Medication interactions to clarify:**

Statins (most commonly atorvastatin or rosuvastatin) interact with large quantities of grapefruit and grapefruit juice, which inhibit the enzyme CYP3A4 and can raise statin blood levels to potentially harmful concentrations. Grapefruit should be avoided or discussed with the prescribing physician. Warfarin or other anticoagulants interact significantly with vitamin K — if the client is on warfarin, vitamin K intake from leafy greens must remain consistent day to day rather than being eliminated, as sudden large changes destabilise INR. ACE inhibitors and potassium-sparing diuretics can cause potassium retention, meaning high-potassium foods need monitoring. Confirm the full medication list before advising on supplementation.

**Referral recommendation:** For a client of this complexity, a referral to a registered dietitian with cardiovascular specialism is strongly advised alongside this plan. The plan below provides a robust, evidence-based framework that you as a trainer can support and reinforce, but clinical dietary management sits within the dietitian's scope.

---

## Caloric Framework

### Estimating Energy Needs

For a 58-year-old male at this activity level, a reasonable starting estimate uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation.

Assuming a body weight of approximately 80–85 kg (adjust for your client's actual weight), height 175 cm:

**Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR):** (10 × weight in kg) + (6.25 × height in cm) − (5 × age) + 5

Using 82 kg: (820) + (1093.75) − (290) + 5 = **approximately 1,629 kcal/day at rest**

**Activity multiplier:** In Phase 1, the client is lightly active (3 sessions per week, low intensity). Apply a multiplier of 1.4. This gives a total daily energy expenditure of approximately **2,280 kcal/day.**

By Phase 3, with four sessions per week at moderate intensity, the multiplier rises to approximately 1.55, giving roughly **2,525 kcal/day.**

**Caloric target:** Unless the cardiologist has specified a weight-loss goal, the aim is not aggressive caloric restriction. Modest weight management — if the client carries excess body fat — is achieved through food quality and composition rather than severe restriction, which would undermine the energy needed for cardiac rehabilitation. A mild deficit of 200–300 kcal/day is appropriate if weight loss is a secondary goal, but this should be confirmed with the medical team.

**Working caloric target across the programme:** 2,100–2,300 kcal/day, adjusted upward in Phase 3 to 2,300–2,500 kcal/day to support increased training volume.

---

## Macronutrient Targets

### Protein

Protein is the most important macronutrient to get right in this population. Post-MI patients undergoing cardiac rehabilitation experience muscle protein synthesis demands from both the exercise stimulus and the physiological recovery process. Older adults also experience anabolic resistance — meaning they require more dietary protein per kilogram of body weight than younger adults to achieve the same muscle protein synthesis response.

**Target: 1.4–1.6 g of protein per kilogram of body weight per day.**

For an 82 kg client, this means **115–131 g of protein daily.** Distribute this across at least four eating occasions rather than concentrating it in one or two meals, as older adults show a blunted muscle protein synthesis response to single large protein doses. Aim for 25–35 g of protein per meal.

**Preferred protein sources (cardiac-friendly):**

Oily fish — salmon, mackerel, sardines, trout — provide protein alongside omega-3 fatty acids and should feature at least three times per week. Skinless poultry — chicken breast, turkey — is lean and versatile. Eggs are an excellent complete protein source; the evidence no longer supports restricting dietary cholesterol from eggs in most cardiac patients, but confirm with the cardiologist if the client has familial hypercholesterolaemia. Legumes — lentils, chickpeas, black beans, kidney beans — provide protein alongside fibre and have a low glycaemic index, making them outstanding cardiac-health foods. Low-fat dairy — Greek yoghurt, cottage cheese, skimmed or semi-skimmed milk — provides high-quality protein and calcium. Plant-based proteins such as tofu, tempeh, and edamame are encouraged, particularly as partial replacements for red meat.

**Protein sources to minimise or avoid:**

Processed red meat — bacon, sausages, salami, deli meats — is strongly associated with increased cardiovascular risk and should be largely eliminated. Unprocessed red meat — lean beef, lamb, pork — can be consumed in moderation (no more than 350–500 g cooked weight per week, per current WHO and British Heart Foundation guidance). Full-fat dairy in large quantities should be moderated due to saturated fat content, though recent evidence is more nuanced — prioritise low-fat versions.

---

### Carbohydrates

**Target: 45–55% of total calories from carbohydrates, emphasising low-glycaemic, high-fibre sources.**

For a 2,200 kcal diet, this means approximately **248–303 g of carbohydrate per day.**

Carbohydrate quality matters enormously in this population. Refined carbohydrates and added sugars drive triglyceride elevation, promote inflammation, and contribute to insulin resistance — all of which are independent cardiovascular risk factors. The focus is on whole-food, fibre-rich carbohydrate sources.

**Preferred carbohydrate sources:**

Oats are a cornerstone of the cardiac nutrition plan. Beta-glucan, the soluble fibre in oats, has robust evidence for LDL cholesterol reduction — consuming 3 g of beta-glucan daily (approximately 75 g of dry rolled oats) can reduce LDL by 5–10%. A bowl of porridge made with rolled oats is an ideal daily breakfast. Sweet potato, new potatoes with skin, and other root vegetables provide slow-release energy with micronutrient density. Brown rice, quinoa, barley, and wholegrain bread provide sustained energy and fibre. Barley in particular contains high levels of beta-glucan and is an underused cardiac superfood — it can be used in soups, stews, and as a rice substitute. Fruit — particularly berries (blueberries, strawberries, raspberries) — provides antioxidants, fibre, and natural sugars with a low glycaemic impact. Aim for two portions of fruit daily. Vegetables of all kinds should be consumed abundantly — aim for at least five portions of vegetables per day, prioritising dark leafy greens, cruciferous vegetables, and colourful varieties.

**Carbohydrate sources to minimise:**

White bread, white rice, and refined pasta in large quantities should be replaced with wholegrain alternatives. Sugary drinks — including fruit juice — should be eliminated. Pastries, biscuits, cakes, and confectionery should be occasional treats rather than regular features. Ultra-processed foods of any kind should be minimised — if a food has more than five ingredients and contains items you would not find in a home kitchen, it warrants scrutiny.

**Peri-workout carbohydrate strategy:**

On training days, a small carbohydrate-containing snack 60–90 minutes before the session helps maintain blood glucose and prevents the fatigue that could compromise exercise safety. A banana with a small amount of nut butter, or a small bowl of porridge, works well. Post-session, a carbohydrate and protein combination within 30–60 minutes supports recovery — a Greek yoghurt with berries and a drizzle of honey, or a small wholegrain wrap with chicken and salad, are practical options.

---

### Fats

**Target: 30–35% of total calories from fat, with a strong emphasis on unsaturated fats and strict limitation of saturated and trans fats.**

For a 2,200 kcal diet, this means approximately **73–86 g of fat per day.**

Fat quality is arguably the most critical macronutrient consideration in post-MI nutrition. The evidence base for the Mediterranean dietary pattern — which is characterised by high unsaturated fat intake, particularly from olive oil and nuts — in secondary cardiovascular prevention is among the strongest in nutritional science. The PREDIMED trial demonstrated a 30% relative risk reduction in major cardiovascular events with a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil or nuts compared to a low-fat control diet.

**Preferred fat sources:**

Extra-virgin olive oil should be the primary cooking and dressing fat. It contains oleocanthal, a natural anti-inflammatory compound, alongside monounsaturated fatty acids that raise HDL and lower LDL. Use it for sautéing at low to medium heat and as a salad dressing. Aim for 2–4 tablespoons daily. Oily fish — salmon, mackerel, sardines, anchovies, herring — provide EPA and DHA, the long-chain omega-3 fatty acids with the strongest evidence for cardiovascular protection. These reduce triglycerides, lower resting heart rate, reduce platelet aggregation, and have anti-arrhythmic properties. Three to four portions per week is the target. Nuts — particularly walnuts, almonds, and pistachios — are outstanding cardiac foods. A 30 g handful daily (approximately 20 almonds or 14 walnut halves) is associated with reduced cardiovascular risk. Walnuts are uniquely high in ALA (plant-based omega-3). Avocado provides monounsaturated fat alongside potassium and fibre. Half an avocado several times per week is a valuable addition. Seeds — flaxseed (ground, for bioavailability), chia seeds, and hemp seeds — provide plant-based omega-3 fatty acids and fibre.

**Fats to strictly limit:**

Saturated fat should be kept below 7% of total calories — approximately 17 g per day for this client. Primary sources to reduce are fatty cuts of red meat, full-fat dairy (butter, cream, full-fat cheese), coconut oil, and palm oil. Trans fats — found in partially hydrogenated vegetable oils and many ultra-processed foods — should be eliminated entirely. They raise LDL, lower HDL, and promote inflammation. Check food labels and avoid any product listing "partially hydrogenated" oil in the ingredients.

---

## The Cardiac Nutrition Pillars

Beyond macronutrients, the following specific dietary strategies have the strongest evidence base for secondary cardiovascular prevention and should be woven into the client's daily eating pattern.

---

### Pillar 1 — The Mediterranean Pattern as the Overarching Framework

Rather than prescribing a rigid meal plan, the Mediterranean dietary pattern provides a flexible, sustainable, and evidence-backed framework. Its key features are: abundant vegetables and fruit, legumes as a protein staple, whole grains, olive oil as the primary fat, regular oily fish, moderate poultry and eggs, limited red meat, limited dairy, and minimal processed foods. Wine is traditionally part of the Mediterranean pattern, but given the client's post-MI status, alcohol should be discussed with the cardiologist — current guidance from the British Heart Foundation and the American Heart Association does not recommend alcohol for cardiovascular benefit, and abstinence or strict moderation (no more than 1–2 units on no more than 5 days per week) is the conservative position.

---

### Pillar 2 — Sodium Management

Excess dietary sodium raises blood pressure, increases cardiac workload, and promotes fluid retention — all of which are particularly harmful post-MI. The target is **no more than 2,000 mg of sodium per day** (approximately 5 g of salt), which aligns with the American Heart Association's recommendation for those with cardiovascular disease.

Practical strategies: Cook from scratch as much as possible, as processed and restaurant foods account for approximately 75% of dietary sodium intake. Use herbs, spices, lemon juice, and vinegar to flavour food instead of salt. When using salt, use a small amount of potassium-enriched salt substitute (LoSalt or similar) — but only if the client is not on potassium-sparing medications (check with the cardiologist). Read food labels — anything above 0.6 g of salt per 100 g is considered high. Tinned fish and vegetables should be chosen in the "no added salt" variety where possible.

---

### Pillar 3 — Dietary Fibre

**Target: 30–35 g of dietary fibre per day.**

Most adults consume approximately 18 g per day. Increasing fibre to 30+ g is associated with significant reductions in LDL cholesterol, improved glycaemic control, reduced blood pressure, and lower all-cause mortality. Soluble fibre specifically — from oats, barley, legumes, apples, and psyllium husk — forms a gel in the gut that binds bile acids (which are made from cholesterol) and removes them from the body, effectively lowering LDL.

Practical daily fibre targets: Breakfast oats (75 g dry) provide approximately 5–6 g. A portion of legumes (150 g cooked lentils) provides approximately 8 g. Five portions of vegetables provide approximately 10–12 g. Two portions of fruit provide approximately 4–6 g. Wholegrain bread or grains provide approximately 4–6 g. Together, these easily reach the 30–35 g target.

**Important note:** If the client is currently eating a low-fibre diet, increase fibre gradually over two to three weeks to avoid gastrointestinal discomfort. Increase water intake alongside fibre increases.

---

### Pillar 4 — Plant Sterols and Stanols

Plant sterols and stanols are naturally occurring compounds found in small amounts in plants that block cholesterol absorption in the gut. Consuming 2 g per day — achievable through fortified foods such as certain margarines (Flora ProActiv, Benecol), fortified yoghurt drinks, or fortified milk — can reduce LDL cholesterol by 10–15% when consumed consistently with meals. This is a meaningful, evidence-based dietary intervention that complements statin therapy. Recommend the client discuss this with their cardiologist and consider incorporating one to two servings of a plant sterol-fortified food daily.

---

### Pillar 5 — Hydration

Adequate hydration is important for cardiovascular function, exercise performance, and medication management. **Target: 2.0–2.5 litres of fluid per day**, increasing to 2.5–3.0 litres on training days.

Water should be the primary fluid. Unsweetened herbal teas are an excellent alternative. Green tea contains catechins with modest evidence for cardiovascular benefit and can replace one to two cups of coffee per day. Caffeine in moderate amounts (up to 300–400 mg per day, equivalent to three to four cups of coffee) is generally safe post-MI, but some cardiologists advise restriction — confirm with the medical team. Sugary drinks, energy drinks, and excessive fruit juice should be eliminated.

---

## Phase-by-Phase Nutrition Focus

The nutritional priorities shift subtly across the three training phases to align with the changing physiological demands.

---

### Phase 1 Nutrition Focus (Weeks 1–4) — Foundation and Habit Building

The primary nutritional goal in Phase 1 mirrors the training goal: establish sustainable habits. Do not overwhelm the client with every change at once. Prioritise the following three changes in the first four weeks.

**Priority 1 — Eliminate the worst offenders.** Processed meats, sugary drinks, trans fats, and excessive salt are removed from the diet in Week 1. These are non-negotiable given the client's cardiac history and represent the highest-impact changes with the clearest evidence base.

**Priority 2 — Build the breakfast habit.** A consistent, cardiac-friendly breakfast sets the nutritional tone for the day and ensures the client has adequate fuel for morning training sessions. The recommended Phase 1 breakfast is a bowl of rolled oat porridge (75 g dry oats cooked in water or semi-skimmed milk) topped with a handful of mixed berries, a tablespoon of ground flaxseed, and a small handful of walnuts. This single meal provides beta-glucan for LDL reduction, omega-3 fatty acids, antioxidants, and approximately 12–15 g of protein if made with milk.

**Priority 3 — Increase oily fish consumption.** If the client is not currently eating oily fish regularly, introduce it in Week 1. Aim for three portions per week. Tinned sardines, tinned mackerel, and tinned salmon are affordable, convenient, and nutritionally equivalent to fresh. A simple lunch of tinned sardines on wholegrain toast with sliced tomato and a drizzle of olive oil is a practical, high-compliance option.

*Breakfast:* Porridge made with 75 g rolled oats and 250 ml semi-skimmed milk, topped with 80 g mixed berries, 1 tablespoon ground flaxseed, 30 g walnuts. Approximate nutrition: 550 kcal, 22 g protein, 65 g carbohydrate, 22 g fat, 9 g fibre.

*Mid-morning snack (on training days, 60–90 minutes pre-session):* 1 medium banana with 1 tablespoon almond butter. Approximate nutrition: 220 kcal, 5 g protein, 30 g carbohydrate, 9 g fat.

*Lunch:* Large mixed salad — 100 g tinned salmon (drained), 80 g chickpeas, cucumber, cherry tomatoes, red onion, spinach, dressed with 1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil and lemon juice. 2 slices wholegrain bread on the side. Approximate nutrition: 520 kcal, 38 g protein, 45 g carbohydrate, 16 g fat, 10 g fibre.

*Afternoon snack:* 150 g low-fat Greek yoghurt with 1 teaspoon honey and a small handful of blueberries. Approximate nutrition: 160 kcal, 15 g protein, 20 g carbohydrate, 2 g fat.

*Dinner:* 150 g baked salmon fillet, 200 g roasted sweet potato (skin on), large portion of steamed broccoli and green beans, drizzled with olive oil and garlic. Approximate nutrition: 580 kcal, 38 g protein, 55 g carbohydrate, 18 g fat, 10 g fibre.

*Post-training recovery snack (if evening session):* 200 ml semi-skimmed milk with a small banana. Approximate nutrition: 180 kcal, 8 g protein, 32 g carbohydrate, 3 g fat.

### Phase 2 Nutrition Focus (Weeks 5–8) — Development and Optimisation

As training volume and intensity increase in Phase 2, nutritional demands shift slightly. Protein intake should be confirmed at the upper end of the target range (1.6 g/kg) to support the increased muscle protein synthesis stimulus. Carbohydrate timing around sessions becomes more important as session duration extends to 40 minutes.

**New Phase 2 nutritional priorities:**

**Introduce legumes as a daily staple.** By Week 5, the client should be incorporating legumes — lentils, chickpeas, black beans, kidney beans — into at least one meal per day. A simple lentil soup, a chickpea curry, or a bean-based chilli provides protein, fibre, slow-release carbohydrate, and potassium in a single dish. Legume consumption is one of the most consistent dietary predictors of cardiovascular longevity across global populations.

**Optimise post-session recovery nutrition.** After resistance sessions in Phase 2, a protein and carbohydrate combination within 30 minutes is important. A practical option is 200 g of low-fat Greek yoghurt (approximately 20 g protein) with a banana and a drizzle of honey. Alternatively, a homemade smoothie: 200 ml semi-skimmed milk, 1 scoop of whey protein (if the client tolerates dairy well), 1 banana, 1 tablespoon of oats, and a handful of spinach (the spinach is undetectable in taste but adds nitrates, which have evidence for blood pressure reduction and exercise performance).

**Introduce a weekly meal planning habit.** By Week 6, encourage the client to plan and prepare meals for the week ahead on a Sunday. Batch cooking a large pot of lentil soup, a tray of roasted vegetables, a portion of brown rice or barley, and marinating fish for the week ahead dramatically increases dietary compliance and reduces reliance on convenience foods.

**Phase 2 sample day of eating (higher training demand):**

*Breakfast:* 2 scrambled eggs on 2 slices of wholegrain toast, with half an avocado and a large handful of spinach wilted in olive oil. Glass of water with a squeeze of lemon. Approximate nutrition: 520 kcal, 28 g protein, 38 g carbohydrate, 28 g fat, 8 g fibre.

*Pre-training snack (90 minutes before session):* 40 g rolled oats made into overnight oats with 150 ml semi-skimmed milk, topped with 1 tablespoon chia seeds and a handful of raspberries. Approximate nutrition: 280 kcal, 14 g protein, 38 g carbohydrate, 7 g fat, 8 g fibre.

*Post-training recovery (within 30 minutes):* 200 g low-fat Greek yoghurt with 1 banana and 1 teaspoon honey. Approximate nutrition: 250 kcal, 20 g protein, 38 g carbohydrate, 2 g fat.

*Lunch:* Large bowl of homemade lentil and vegetable soup (200 g cooked red lentils, carrots, celery, onion, tinned tomatoes, cumin, turmeric, low-sodium vegetable stock) with 1 slice wholegrain bread. Approximate nutrition: 480 kcal, 28 g protein, 72 g carbohydrate, 6 g fat, 14 g fibre.

*Afternoon snack:* 30 g mixed nuts (walnuts, almonds, pistachios) with an apple. Approximate nutrition: 230 kcal, 6 g protein, 22 g carbohydrate, 14 g fat, 5 g fibre.

*Dinner:* 150 g grilled mackerel fillet, 150 g cooked barley, large mixed roasted vegetable medley (courgette, red pepper, aubergine, cherry tomatoes, red onion) roasted in olive oil with herbs. Approximate nutrition: 620 kcal, 38 g protein, 58 g carbohydrate, 22 g fat, 12 g fibre.

**Phase 2 daily totals (training day):** Approximately 2,380 kcal | 134 g protein | 266 g carbohydrate | 79 g fat | 47 g fibre.

### Phase 3 Nutrition Focus (Weeks 9–12) — Consolidation and Long-Term Sustainability

Phase 3 nutrition shifts focus from habit installation to long-term sustainability. The client should now have a solid dietary foundation. The goal is to ensure the eating pattern is genuinely enjoyable, socially compatible, and maintainable for life — because the cardiovascular benefit of dietary change is only realised if it is sustained indefinitely.

**New Phase 3 nutritional priorities:**

**Social eating and restaurant strategies.** Discuss how the client navigates eating out, social occasions, and travel. Practical strategies: choose fish or chicken dishes over red meat at restaurants, ask for sauces on the side, choose olive oil and vinegar over creamy dressings, opt for vegetables or salad instead of chips, and avoid the bread basket. The 80/20 principle applies — if the client eats well 80% of the time, occasional deviations will not meaningfully affect cardiovascular outcomes.

**Reassess and adjust caloric intake.** By Week 9, the client's body composition may have changed. If weight has decreased, caloric intake may need to increase slightly

# Supplementary Strength Development Component
### Integrated into the 12-Week Post-MI Cardiac Conditioning Programme

---

## Clinical Preamble — Strength Training Post-MI

Before expanding the resistance training component, it is worth being explicit about why strength work is both safe and important for this client, and what the governing rules are, because the evidence base has shifted considerably in recent years and some clients — and indeed some clinicians — still carry the outdated assumption that post-MI patients should avoid resistance training entirely.

The American Heart Association formally endorsed resistance training as a component of cardiac rehabilitation in 2007, and subsequent research has consistently demonstrated that appropriately dosed strength training reduces cardiovascular mortality, improves insulin sensitivity, lowers resting blood pressure, increases lean muscle mass (which is independently protective against cardiac events), and improves the functional capacity needed for daily life. For a 58-year-old male who is feeling deconditioned, the loss of muscle mass — sarcopenia — is a genuine health risk that compounds the cardiac risk. Addressing it is not optional.

The non-negotiables remain unchanged and must be reinforced with every session.

**Absolute rules for all strength work:**

No Valsalva manoeuvre under any circumstances. The intrathoracic pressure spike produced by a breath-hold during exertion can acutely elevate blood pressure by 40–50 mmHg and dramatically increase cardiac afterload. Exhale on every effort, every repetition, every set, without exception. If you observe the client holding their breath — even briefly — stop the set, reset, and re-cue before continuing.

Heart rate ceiling of 115 bpm remains in force. Check HR at the end of every working set. If HR exceeds 115 bpm, extend the rest period until it returns below 100 bpm before the next set. If HR does not recover within three minutes, end the session.

No maximal or near-maximal effort. Loads should never exceed what the client could lift for at least four to five more reps beyond the prescribed rep count — this is an RPE ceiling of approximately 13/20 ("somewhat hard") and an RIR (reps in reserve) floor of four. This is not a programme about finding limits. It is a programme about building a foundation.

No isometric holds under load. Sustained isometric contractions — such as holding a heavy squat at the bottom — produce prolonged pressure responses that are inappropriate for this population. All exercises should involve continuous, controlled movement.

No overhead pressing with heavy loads in the early weeks. Overhead pressing increases intrathoracic pressure more than most other movements and should be kept light and progressed conservatively.

No supine exercises with very heavy dumbbells that require the client to hoist the weight into position unassisted — the effort of getting into position can spike HR and blood pressure before the set even begins.

---

## Why He Feels Deconditioned — and What That Means for Programming

Six months post-MI, deconditioning is almost universal and has multiple overlapping causes. The acute hospitalisation period involves bed rest and significant physical inactivity. The psychological impact of a cardiac event — fear of exertion, anxiety about triggering another event — leads many patients to dramatically reduce their activity levels for months afterward. Beta-blockers, which most post-MI patients take, reduce exercise capacity and can contribute to fatigue. The inflammatory response associated with myocardial injury accelerates muscle protein breakdown. The result is a client who may have lost meaningful amounts of lean muscle mass, strength, and neuromuscular coordination in a relatively short period.

The good news is that deconditioning responds rapidly to appropriate training stimulus. Neuromuscular adaptations — the nervous system learning to recruit muscle fibres more efficiently — occur within the first two to four weeks and produce strength gains before any significant muscle hypertrophy takes place. This means the client will feel meaningfully stronger relatively quickly, which is important for motivation and confidence. Frame this for him: early strength gains are real, they are happening in the nervous system, and they are the foundation for everything that follows.

---

## Revised Programme Structure with Expanded Strength Component

The original programme's three-phase architecture is preserved. What changes is the resistance training content within each phase — exercises are more deliberately selected for strength development, loading parameters are more explicitly progressive, and a dedicated strength-focused session is added to the weekly structure from Phase 2 onward. The cardiovascular conditioning sessions and nutrition plan remain as previously described.

The revised weekly session structure is as follows.

**Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4):** Three sessions per week. All three sessions now have a dual purpose — movement quality and foundational strength. The original programme's resistance sessions are retained but with more explicit loading guidance and the addition of a primary compound movement to each session.

**Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8):** Four sessions per week. Two sessions are dedicated strength sessions with a cardiovascular warm-up. One session is dedicated cardiovascular conditioning. One session is active recovery. This represents a meaningful shift toward strength as a primary training outcome.

**Phase 3 (Weeks 9–12):** Four sessions per week. Two sessions are progressive strength sessions. One session is cardiovascular conditioning. One session is active recovery with mobility work. Loads in Phase 3 are the heaviest of the programme — still well within safe parameters, but representing genuine strength stimulus.

---

---

# PHASE 1 — FOUNDATIONAL STRENGTH (Weeks 1–4)

## Programming Philosophy for Phase 1

The primary goal of Phase 1 strength work is not to produce maximal strength gains — it is to teach the client's nervous system how to produce force safely, to establish the breathing pattern as automatic, to identify any movement limitations that need addressing, and to build the connective tissue tolerance that precedes meaningful loading. Tendons, ligaments, and joint cartilage adapt more slowly than muscle and the nervous system. Rushing load progression in the first four weeks is the most common programming error with deconditioned clients and leads to joint pain that derails the programme entirely.

Think of Phase 1 as building the scaffolding. The building comes later.

**Phase 1 strength parameters:**
- Sets: 2–3
- Reps: 12–15
- Load: RPE 10–12 (light to fairly light), minimum 4 reps in reserve at all times
- Rest: 90–120 seconds between sets
- Tempo: Controlled — approximately 2 seconds on the lowering phase, 1 second pause, 1–2 seconds on the lifting phase. No bouncing, no momentum.
- HR check: After every set

---

### Week 1 — Revised Strength Sessions

The original Week 1 sessions are restructured to include one primary compound movement per session as the anchor exercise. Everything else supports it.

---

**Session 1 — Lower Body Strength Focus**

*Warm-up (10 minutes):*
5 minutes recumbent bike at minimal resistance. Then: 10 bodyweight squats to a high box (movement rehearsal, not a working set), 10 hip circles each direction, 10 glute bridges lying on the floor (feet flat, drive hips to ceiling, squeeze glutes at the top — this activates the posterior chain and is an excellent low-HR warm-up movement), 10 ankle circles each direction.

*Primary compound movement:*

**Leg press** — This is the anchor lower body strength exercise for Phase 1. The leg press is chosen over the squat as the primary movement for several reasons: it eliminates the balance and spinal loading demands of a barbell squat, it allows precise load control, it keeps the client in a supported position, and it produces a very predictable HR response. It is not a permanent substitute for free-standing squat patterns — those are developed progressively — but it is the right starting point.

3 sets × 12 reps. Feet hip-width apart, toes slightly out, positioned in the middle of the platform. Press through the whole foot — do not rise onto the toes. Do not lock the knees at the top. Lower under control for 2 seconds. Exhale on the press, inhale on the lower. Load: start conservatively — the client should feel the effort but be nowhere near failure. Check HR after each set. Rest 2 minutes between sets.

*Supporting exercises:*

**Glute bridge (floor)** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Lie on the floor, knees bent, feet flat. Drive the hips to the ceiling by squeezing the glutes — do not hyperextend the lower back. Hold for 1 second at the top. Lower with control. Exhale on the drive up. This is a foundational posterior chain exercise that is extremely low-risk and highly effective for activating the glutes, which are typically inhibited in deconditioned individuals who spend significant time seated. Progress to a single-leg version in later weeks.

**Seated leg curl** — 2 sets × 15 reps. Light load. Exhale on the curl.

**Seated calf raise** — 2 sets × 20 reps. Bodyweight or light plate on thighs. Full range of motion — lower the heel below the platform level if possible to stretch the calf, then rise fully onto the ball of the foot. This promotes lower-limb circulation and venous return, which is particularly valuable post-MI.

**Dead bug** — 2 sets × 8 reps each side. Continuous breathing throughout. This is the core exercise for every lower body session in Phase 1.

*Cool-down:* 5 minutes slow treadmill walk. Stretches: standing hip flexor lunge (30 seconds each side), supine hamstring stretch (30 seconds each side), seated calf stretch (30 seconds each side).

---

**Session 2 — Cardiovascular Conditioning**

As per the original programme — 20 minutes recumbent bike, HR 95–108 bpm. No changes to this session.

---

**Session 3 — Upper Body Strength Focus**

*Warm-up (10 minutes):*
5 minutes recumbent bike. Then: 10 arm circles each direction, 10 wall slides (arms slide up a wall, elbows bent to 90 degrees, press the arms overhead while keeping the back of the hands and elbows in contact with the wall — this opens the chest and activates the lower trapezius), 10 band pull-aparts (light resistance band held in both hands at shoulder height, pull the band apart by squeezing the shoulder blades together — excellent for posterior shoulder health and posture correction).

*Primary compound movement:*

**Seated cable row (close grip, neutral handles)** — This is the anchor upper body strength exercise for Phase 1. Pulling movements are prioritised over pushing movements in the early weeks for two reasons. First, post-MI patients frequently have poor thoracic posture from the protective hunching response to chest pain and hospitalisation — rowing movements directly address this by strengthening the mid-back and retracting the shoulder blades. Second, pulling movements generally produce a lower HR response than pressing movements of equivalent effort, making them safer in the early weeks.

3 sets × 12 reps. Sit tall — do not round the lower back. Initiate the movement by retracting the shoulder blades before bending the elbows. Pull the handles to the lower sternum. Return with control. Exhale on the pull, inhale on the return. Light to moderate load. Rest 2 minutes between sets.

*Supporting exercises:*

**Chest press machine** — 2 sets × 15 reps. Machine rather than free weights in Week 1 — the guided path reduces stabilisation demand and keeps effort controlled. Light load. Exhale on the press.

**Lat pulldown (wide grip, to chin)** — 2 sets × 15 reps. Do not pull behind the neck. Lean back very slightly — approximately 10–15 degrees — and pull the bar to the upper chest. Exhale on the pull-down.

**Dumbbell shoulder press (seated)** — 2 sets × 12 reps. Very light load (3–5 kg). Seated to eliminate the balance demand. Exhale on the press.

**Band pull-apart** — 2 sets × 15 reps. Light resistance band. Arms straight at shoulder height, pull the band apart until the arms are in a T position, squeezing the shoulder blades together. This is a postural corrective exercise as much as a strength exercise and should be included in every upper body session throughout the programme.

**Modified push-up (from knees or against a wall)** — 2 sets × 10 reps. Begin with wall push-ups if the client cannot perform a knee push-up with continuous breathing and controlled tempo. The push-up is a fundamental human movement pattern and the goal is to progress to a full push-up by the end of the programme. Exhale on the push away from the wall or floor.

*Cool-down:* 5 minutes slow treadmill walk. Stretches: chest doorway stretch (30 seconds), lat stretch with arm overhead against wall (30 seconds each side), neck side flexion (20 seconds each side — gentle, no overpressure).

---

### Week 2 — Strength Progression

**Progression principle for Week 2:** Add one set to each primary compound movement (moving from 3 to the working volume). On supporting exercises, add one set where HR data from Week 1 confirms the client has headroom. Do not increase load yet — the priority is volume tolerance before load progression.

**Session 1 — Lower Body Strength Focus (Week 2)**

*Primary:*
**Leg press** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Same load as Week 1 unless HR was consistently below 105 bpm after each set, in which case a small increment (5 kg on the machine stack) is appropriate.

*New addition:*
**Goblet squat (to high box)** — 2 sets × 10 reps. Introduce the free-standing squat pattern alongside the leg press. Use a light dumbbell (4–6 kg) or no weight. The box height should allow the client to sit back comfortably without losing the lumbar curve. This is a movement quality exercise — load is irrelevant. Exhale on the stand. The goal is to establish the pattern so it can be loaded progressively in later phases.

*Supporting exercises:* Same as Week 1, with one additional set on the glute bridge (3 sets × 15 reps).

---

**Session 3 — Upper Body Strength Focus (Week 2)**

*Primary:*
**Seated cable row** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Same load as Week 1 or small increase if HR allows.

*New addition:*
**Dumbbell chest press (flat bench)** — 2 sets × 12 reps. Transition one set from the chest press machine to dumbbells. Use a light load. The dumbbell version requires more stabilisation and begins to develop the shoulder girdle musculature more completely. Exhale on the press. Keep the dumbbells at chest level — do not lower them below the chest, which would place excessive stress on the anterior shoulder capsule.

*Supporting exercises:* Same as Week 1, with one additional set on the lat pulldown.

---

### Week 3 — Load Introduction

**Progression principle for Week 3:** This is the first week where load increases are the primary progression variable, rather than volume. Volume stays the same as Week 2. Load increases by the smallest available increment on the primary compound movements where the client has demonstrated consistent form and HR response within limits.

**Session 1 — Lower Body Strength Focus (Week 3)**

*Primary:*
**Leg press** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Increase load by 5–10 kg if Week 2 HR data supports it.

**Goblet squat (to box)** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Add 2 kg to the dumbbell if the movement pattern is solid. Begin to lower the box height slightly — moving toward a parallel squat depth over the coming weeks.

*New addition:*
**Single-leg glute bridge** — 2 sets × 10 reps each leg. Progress from the bilateral glute bridge. One foot flat on the floor, the other leg extended or bent with the foot lifted. Drive the hips up through the planted foot. This is a significant progression in posterior chain demand and also challenges hip stability. Exhale on the drive up.

*Supporting exercises:* Same as Week 2.

---

**Session 3 — Upper Body Strength Focus (Week 3)**

*Primary:*
**Seated cable row** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Increase load modestly. Dropping from 12 to 10 reps allows a load increase while keeping effort controlled.

**Dumbbell chest press** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Increase load by 1–2 kg if Week 2 HR data supports it.

*New addition:*
**Dumbbell Romanian deadlift (RDL)** — 2 sets × 12 reps. Introduce the hip hinge pattern in the upper body session as a posterior chain complement. Use light dumbbells (8–10 kg). Hinge at the hips, soft knee bend, dumbbells track close to the legs, feel the hamstring stretch, return to standing by driving the hips forward. Exhale on the return to standing. This is one of the most important movement patterns for daily life and will be progressively loaded throughout the programme.

*Supporting exercises:* Same as Week 2. Progress the push-up — if the client has been doing wall push-ups, move to an incline push-up (hands on a bench or step). If already on knees, attempt 2 reps of a full push-up at the end of each set.

---

### Week 4 — Deload and Assessment

As per the original programme — volume reduces by 30%, load stays the same, movement quality is reviewed. Re-run baseline assessments. Add a specific strength assessment: record the load used on the leg press and seated cable row for 12 reps with good form and HR below 110 bpm. This becomes the Phase 1 strength baseline against which Phase 2 and Phase 3 progress is measured.

# PHASE 2 — STRENGTH DEVELOPMENT (Weeks 5–8)

## Programming Philosophy for Phase 2

Phase 2 is where genuine strength development begins. The nervous system adaptations from Phase 1 mean the client is now more efficient at recruiting muscle fibres, and the connective tissue has had four weeks to begin adapting to load. The rep range drops, the load increases, and the exercise selection becomes more demanding — introducing free-weight compound movements that require greater coordination and produce a stronger strength stimulus.

The fourth session per week is now a dedicated strength session rather than an active recovery session. Active recovery is incorporated as a shorter component within the week rather than a full session, or on a rest day as a 20-minute home walk.

**Phase 2 strength parameters:**
- Sets: 3–4
- Reps: 8–12
- Load: RPE 12–13 (fairly light to somewhat hard), minimum 4 reps in reserve
- Rest: 2 minutes between sets on compound movements, 90 seconds on accessory exercises
- Tempo: 3 seconds lowering, 1 second pause, 1–2 seconds lifting on compound movements
- HR check: After every set

**Session structure for Phase 2:**
- Session 1: Lower body strength
- Session 2: Upper body strength
- Session 3: Cardiovascular conditioning
- Session 4: Full body strength (lighter, higher rep — bridges the two strength sessions)

---

### Week 5

---

**Session 1 — Lower Body Strength (Week 5)**

*Warm-up (12 minutes):*
5 minutes recumbent bike. Then: 10 bodyweight squats (full depth if possible), 10 single-leg glute bridges each side, 10 lateral band walks each direction (light resistance band around the ankles, step sideways 10 steps, return — activates the hip abductors which are critical for knee stability during squatting and stepping movements), 10 hip circles each direction.

*Primary compound movement:*

**Goblet squat (free-standing, no box)** — 4 sets × 10 reps. This is the progression from the box squat. The client now squats to full depth (or as deep as mobility allows without losing the lumbar curve). Use a dumbbell of 8–12 kg. Feet hip-width apart, toes out 15–30 degrees, chest tall, elbows inside the knees at the bottom. Exhale on the stand. This is a genuine strength exercise now — not just a movement pattern drill. Rest 2 minutes between sets.

*Secondary compound movement:*

**Dumbbell Romanian deadlift** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Load increase from Phase 1. Use 12–16 kg dumbbells depending on the client's Phase 1 baseline. This is now a strength exercise, not just a pattern introduction. Controlled 3-second lowering phase. Exhale on the return to standing. Rest 2 minutes.

*Accessory exercises:*

**Leg press** — 2 sets × 12 reps. Now used as an accessory rather than the primary movement. Load increase from Phase 1 end-point.

**Single-leg glute bridge** — 3 sets × 12 reps each leg. Add a light dumbbell across the hips if the client can maintain form and HR stays within limits.

**Seated calf raise** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Add a light plate on the thighs for resistance.

**Dead bug** — 3 sets × 10 reps each side.

*Cool-down:* 5 minutes treadmill walk. Stretches: hip flexor lunge (45 seconds each side), pigeon pose or figure-four stretch for the glutes (45 seconds each side), hamstring stretch (45 seconds each side).

---

**Session 2 — Upper Body Strength (Week 5)**

*Warm-up (12 minutes):*
5 minutes recumbent bike. Then: 15 band pull-aparts, 10 wall slides, 10 arm circles each direction, 10 scapular push-ups (in a push-up position, without bending the elbows, protract and retract the shoulder blades — this activates the serratus anterior and prepares the shoulder girdle for pressing).

*Primary compound movement:*

**Dumbbell chest press (flat bench)** — 4 sets × 10 reps. Load increase from Phase 1. This is now the primary pressing movement. Use a load that allows 10 controlled reps with 4 reps in reserve. Exhale on the press. Lower the dumbbells to chest level with a 3-second eccentric. Rest 2 minutes between sets.

*Secondary compound movement:*

**Seated cable row (wide grip, overhand)** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Change the grip from the Phase 1 close neutral grip to a wide overhand grip. This shifts more emphasis to the mid-trapezius and rhomboids, which are important for postural correction. Load increase from Phase 1. Rest 2 minutes.

*Accessory exercises:*

**Lat pulldown** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Load increase from Phase 1.

**Dumbbell shoulder press (seated)** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Load increase from Phase 1. Keep the load conservative — overhead pressing produces a higher HR response than most other upper body movements.

**Dumbbell lateral raise** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Light load (4–6 kg). Controlled movement — raise to shoulder height, lower with control over 3 seconds. Do not swing the weight.

**Incline push-up (hands on bench)** — 3 sets × 10–12 reps. Progress from the modified push-up. The incline reduces the percentage of bodyweight being pressed, making it more manageable than a full push-up while being more demanding than a wall push-up. Exhale on the push.

**Band pull-apart** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Every upper body session.

*Cool-down:* 5 minutes treadmill walk. Stretches: chest doorway stretch (45 seconds), lat stretch (45 seconds each side), posterior shoulder stretch — bring one arm across the chest and hold (30 seconds each side).

---

**Session 3 — Cardiovascular Conditioning (Week 5)**

As per the original programme — 35 minutes combining recumbent bike, treadmill, and upright bike. No changes.

---

**Session 4 — Full Body Strength, Higher Rep (Week 5)**

This session bridges the two dedicated strength sessions. It uses lighter loads and higher reps, targeting the whole body in a single session. It functions as both a strength stimulus and an active recovery session — the lighter loading allows the body to move through full ranges of motion and promotes blood flow to recovering tissues without adding significant fatigue.

**Full body session parameters:** 2–3 sets × 15 reps | RPE 10–11 | Rest 60–90 seconds | HR ceiling 108 bpm (lower than other sessions — this is a recovery-oriented session).

*Warm-up:* 10 minutes — 5 minutes recumbent bike, 5 minutes mobility.

*Exercises:*

**Leg press** — 2 sets × 15 reps. Light load — approximately 60% of what was used in Session 1

# Phase III Cardiac Clearance — Programme Progression
### Weeks 8–12: Revised and Expanded

---

## Clinical Transition Brief

This is a significant milestone and worth framing carefully for both you and your client. Phase III cardiac rehabilitation clearance represents the cardiologist's confidence that the myocardium has remodelled sufficiently, that the client's cardiovascular response to exercise is stable and predictable, and that the risk profile has shifted meaningfully in a positive direction. It does not mean the client is back to pre-MI baseline — it means the guardrails can be widened under continued professional supervision.

**What has changed with Phase III clearance:**

The heart rate ceiling rises from 115 bpm to approximately **136 bpm** (85% of age-predicted maximum of 220 − 58 = 162 bpm). In practice, programme targets will sit at **125–132 bpm** during peak effort — approaching but not routinely hitting the ceiling, which remains a hard stop. This is a meaningful increase that opens up a substantially wider range of exercise intensities.

Moderate Valsalva at moderate loads is now permitted. This requires careful definition. The cardiologist's clearance does not mean uninhibited breath-holding under heavy load — it means that the brief, natural intra-abdominal pressure increase that occurs during moderate exertion is acceptable. In practical terms, this means the client can use a **short, controlled breath-hold of no more than one to two seconds** during the sticking point of a moderate-load compound lift, followed immediately by a controlled exhale. This is categorically different from a full Valsalva under near-maximal load. The continuous breathing pattern remains the default — the modified Valsalva is a tool for moderate compound lifts only, not a licence to abandon breathing discipline across the board.

No maximal effort remains absolute. The RPE ceiling rises from 13 to **15/20** ("hard") with a minimum of **3 reps in reserve** on all sets. The client should never approach muscular failure.

**New parameters summary:**

| Parameter | Phase I–II | Phase III |
|---|---|---|
| HR ceiling | 115 bpm | 136 bpm (target 125–132) |
| RPE ceiling | 13/20 | 15/20 |
| Reps in reserve | 4+ | 3+ |
| Valsalva | None | Brief, moderate loads only |
| Max effort | Prohibited | Prohibited |
| Rest between sets | 90–120 sec | 2–3 minutes compound, 90 sec accessory |

---

## Transition Week — End of Week 8

Before launching into the revised programme, use the final session of Week 8 as a **transition assessment session**. This is not a testing session in the maximal sense — it is a calibration session to establish new working loads under the expanded parameters.

**Transition assessment protocol:**

For each primary compound movement, perform the following. Take the load used for the final working set of Week 8. Perform one set of 8 reps at that load, monitoring HR throughout. Rest 3 minutes. If HR recovered below 105 bpm and RPE was below 13, add a modest load increment and perform another set of 6 reps. Record the load, HR response, and RPE. This gives you a calibrated starting point for Phase III loading without exposing the client to an abrupt jump in demand.

**Movements to assess:**
- Goblet squat or front squat (see below)
- Dumbbell Romanian deadlift
- Dumbbell chest press
- Seated cable row
- Lat pulldown
- Dumbbell shoulder press

Record everything. These numbers are your Phase III baselines.

---

## Revised Nutrition Adjustments for Phase III

Before detailing the training programme, note that the expanded training stimulus of Phase III warrants a nutritional recalibration.

**Caloric adjustment:** Increase daily caloric intake by 150–200 kcal on training days to support the higher training volume and intensity. This comes primarily from additional carbohydrate — add one extra serving of a complex carbohydrate source (an additional portion of oats, sweet potato, brown rice, or barley) either pre- or post-training.

**Protein:** Maintain at 1.6 g/kg bodyweight. With increased training intensity, the muscle protein synthesis stimulus is greater, and consistent protein intake becomes even more important. Ensure the client is hitting protein targets on rest days as well as training days — muscle repair happens during recovery, not during the session.

**Pre-training nutrition:** With HR now permitted to reach 125–132 bpm during peak effort, the pre-training meal becomes more important for performance and safety. A carbohydrate and protein meal 90–120 minutes before training — such as chicken and rice, or Greek yoghurt with oats and banana — ensures blood glucose is stable during higher-intensity work. Exercising in a fasted or hypoglycaemic state at Phase III intensities is not appropriate for this client.

**Creatine monohydrate:** This is worth raising with the cardiologist at the Phase III transition. Creatine monohydrate at 3–5 g per day has a growing evidence base for cardiovascular safety and may support the increased strength training demands of Phase III. A 2021 review in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition found no adverse cardiovascular effects in cardiac populations at standard doses. This is a conversation for the medical team, not a unilateral recommendation — but it is worth initiating.

# WEEK 8 (TRANSITION) — FINAL PHASE II SESSION AND CALIBRATION

Use the last session of Week 8 as described in the transition assessment protocol above. Keep training volume low — two sets per exercise, moderate load, focus entirely on HR response and movement quality at slightly elevated intensity. Introduce the client to the concept of the modified Valsalva in a controlled setting: during the dumbbell chest press, cue a brief natural breath-hold at the sticking point (the point of greatest mechanical disadvantage, typically just off the chest), followed immediately by a controlled exhale through the completion of the rep. Practise this for two sets before it appears in a working context.

# PHASE 3 — CONSOLIDATION AND STRENGTH (Weeks 9–12)

## Programming Philosophy

Phase III training has three concurrent goals that must be held in balance simultaneously.

**Goal one — meaningful strength development.** With the expanded HR ceiling and modified Valsalva permission, loads can now enter a range that produces genuine hypertrophic and neuromuscular adaptation. The client will build real strength in this phase — not just functional capacity, but measurable increases in the force-producing capability of the major muscle groups. This directly addresses the deconditioning he presented with and has independent cardiovascular protective effects through improved insulin sensitivity, reduced visceral adiposity, and enhanced metabolic health.

**Goal two — cardiovascular progression.** The higher HR ceiling allows the introduction of moderate-intensity interval training on the cardiovascular sessions — a significant upgrade from the brisk walking intervals of Phase II. Moderate-intensity intervals at 125–130 bpm produce substantially greater improvements in VO2 max than steady-state work at 100–108 bpm, and VO2 max is one of the strongest independent predictors of cardiovascular mortality. Every 1 MET increase in cardiorespiratory fitness is associated with approximately a 13% reduction in all-cause mortality in cardiac populations.

**Goal three — independence and sustainability.** By Week 12, the client should be capable of training with minimal supervision, understanding his own HR response, knowing how to self-regulate intensity, and having a programme he can continue beyond the formal 12-week block. The final two weeks deliberately introduce more client autonomy — you are present but increasingly in a coaching rather than directing role.

**Phase III session structure (four sessions per week):**
- **Session A:** Lower body strength — primary focus
- **Session B:** Upper body strength — primary focus
- **Session C:** Cardiovascular conditioning — moderate intensity intervals
- **Session D:** Full body strength circuit — moderate load, higher rep, metabolic component

---

## Exercise Progressions Introduced in Phase III

Several new exercises and progressions are introduced in Phase III that were not appropriate in earlier phases. Each is justified below.

**Barbell back squat (low load):** The barbell squat is introduced in Week 10 as a progression from the goblet squat. It is not introduced earlier because the goblet squat must first demonstrate consistent form, adequate hip and ankle mobility, and a predictable HR response. The barbell squat allows greater loading potential and is a more complete lower body strength stimulus. Loads in Phase III will remain moderate — the goal is not a heavy squat, it is a technically sound squat with a load that produces genuine strength adaptation. The modified Valsalva is appropriate here at moderate loads.

**Trap bar deadlift:** The trap bar (hex bar) deadlift is introduced in Week 9 as a progression from the dumbbell RDL. The trap bar places the load at the client's sides rather than in front of the body, reducing the moment arm on the lumbar spine compared to a conventional barbell deadlift, while allowing substantially greater loading than dumbbells. It is the safest and most appropriate deadlift variation for this population and produces excellent whole-body strength stimulus.

**Dumbbell incline chest press:** Introduced in Week 9 as a variation on the flat dumbbell press. The incline angle increases upper pectoral and anterior deltoid recruitment and provides variety that prevents accommodation.

**Cable face pull:** Introduced in Week 9 as a replacement for the band pull-apart. The cable provides consistent tension throughout the range of motion and allows progressive loading. The face pull targets the posterior deltoid, external rotators, and mid-trapezius — critical muscles for shoulder health and postural correction that are chronically underworked in most adults.

**Assisted pull-up or negative pull-up:** Introduced in Week 11 as a progression from the lat pulldown. The pull-up is a more demanding and complete upper body pulling movement. The assisted version (using a resistance band looped over the bar, or an assisted pull-up machine) allows the client to experience the movement pattern with reduced load. Negative pull-ups (jumping to the top position and lowering slowly) develop eccentric strength. This is an aspirational progression — include it only if the client's strength and HR response support it.

**Moderate-intensity treadmill intervals:** Introduced in Week 9 on the cardiovascular session. Work intervals now target 122–130 bpm rather than the previous 108–113 bpm ceiling. This is a genuine moderate-intensity cardiovascular stimulus.

---

### WEEK 9

**Theme:** Introduce Phase III loads and new exercises. Establish new working weights. Monitor HR response carefully at the higher intensity — the first week at Phase III parameters is a data-collection week as much as a training week.

---

**Session A — Lower Body Strength (Week 9)**

*Warm-up (12 minutes):*
5 minutes upright stationary bike at light resistance, cadence 80–90 rpm. Then: 15 lateral band walks each direction, 10 bodyweight squats (full depth), 10 single-leg glute bridges each side, 10 hip circles each direction, 10 ankle dorsiflexion mobilisations (stand facing a wall, drive the knee forward over the toes while keeping the heel flat — improves ankle mobility for squatting).

*Primary compound movement:*

**Trap bar deadlift** — 4 sets × 8 reps. This is the new anchor lower body exercise. Set up with the feet hip-width apart inside the trap bar, hinge at the hips to grip the handles, establish a neutral spine (not rounded, not hyperextended), take a breath and brace the abdomen moderately — this is where the modified Valsalva applies: a brief, controlled intra-abdominal brace of one to two seconds through the initial pull, then exhale as the hips extend and the bar clears the floor. Do not hold the breath for the entire rep. Lower with control — 3 seconds on the way down. Rest 3 minutes between sets.

**Load guidance:** Begin conservatively. If the client's dumbbell RDL working weight was 16 kg per hand (32 kg total), start the trap bar at 40–50 kg including the bar weight. The trap bar itself typically weighs 20–25 kg — factor this in. The goal in Week 9 is to find a load that produces RPE 12–13 for 8 reps with 3–4 reps in reserve. Check HR after each set — it will be higher than previous lower body sessions. If HR exceeds 128 bpm after a set, extend the rest period to 4 minutes before the next set.

*Secondary compound movement:*

**Goblet squat** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Increase load from Phase II end-point. Use 16–20 kg dumbbell depending on the client's Phase II baseline. Full depth. Exhale on the stand. The modified Valsalva is not needed here — the goblet squat load is moderate enough that continuous breathing is maintained. Rest 2 minutes.

*Accessory exercises:*

**Bulgarian split squat (rear foot elevated, bodyweight or light dumbbells)** — 3 sets × 8 reps each leg. This is a new exercise in Phase III. The Bulgarian split squat is a unilateral lower body exercise that develops single-leg strength, hip flexor mobility, and balance simultaneously. Place the rear foot on a bench (approximately 45 cm high), front foot approximately 60–70 cm forward. Lower the rear knee toward the floor under control — 3 seconds down — then drive back up through the front foot. Exhale on the drive up. Begin with bodyweight only. This exercise will produce a higher HR response than bilateral exercises — monitor carefully. Rest 90 seconds between legs.

**Single-leg glute bridge with dumbbell** — 3 sets × 12 reps each leg. Place a light dumbbell across the hips. Drive up through the planted foot, squeeze the glute at the top. Exhale on the drive up.

**Leg curl (seated machine)** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Load increase from Phase II.

**Pallof press (cable, standing)** — 3 sets × 10 reps each side. This is a new core exercise replacing the dead bug as the primary core movement in Phase III. Set a cable pulley to chest height. Stand side-on to the cable, feet shoulder-width apart. Hold the handle at the chest with both hands. Press the handle straight out in front of you, hold for 2 seconds, return to the chest. The cable pulls you toward it — resist this rotation. This is an anti-rotation core exercise that develops the deep stabilisers without any breath-holding risk. Exhale on the press out. Rest 60 seconds between sides.

*Cool-down:* 5 minutes treadmill walk at 3.0 km/h. Stretches: hip flexor lunge with thoracic rotation (45 seconds each side — in the lunge position, rotate the torso toward the front leg and reach the same-side arm to the ceiling), pigeon pose (60 seconds each side), hamstring stretch (45 seconds each side), calf stretch (45 seconds each side).

---

**Session B — Upper Body Strength (Week 9)**

*Warm-up (12 minutes):*
5 minutes upright bike. Then: 15 band pull-aparts, 10 wall slides, 10 scapular push-ups, 10 external rotation with band (band anchored at elbow height, elbow bent to 90 degrees, rotate the forearm outward — 10 reps each side. This warms up the rotator cuff and is an important injury prevention exercise for anyone doing significant pressing volume).

*Primary compound movement:*

**Dumbbell incline chest press** — 4 sets × 8 reps. Set the bench to 30–45 degrees. This is a new exercise — begin at a load slightly below the flat press working weight from Phase II, as the incline changes the mechanics and the client will need a session or two to calibrate. Exhale on the press, with a brief moderate brace at the sticking point (just off the chest) if needed — this is where the modified Valsalva applies on pressing movements. Lower with control over 3 seconds. Rest 3 minutes between sets.

*Secondary compound movement:*

**Seated cable row (close grip, neutral)** — 4 sets × 8 reps. Load increase from Phase II. This is now a genuine strength set — the load should produce RPE 13 for 8 reps with 3–4 reps in reserve. Initiate with the shoulder blades, pull to the lower sternum, control the return over 3 seconds. Brief brace at the point of maximum pull is acceptable. Rest 2–3 minutes.

*Accessory exercises:*

**Lat pulldown** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Load increase from Phase II.

**Cable face pull** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Set the cable pulley to face height. Use a rope attachment. Pull the rope toward the face, separating the hands as you pull so the thumbs finish pointing behind you. Elbows stay high throughout. This is a postural corrective and shoulder health exercise — do not load it heavily. The movement should feel like a controlled squeeze of the posterior shoulder and mid-back. Exhale on the pull. Rest 60 seconds.

**Dumbbell shoulder press (seated)** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Load increase from Phase II. Monitor HR carefully — overhead pressing at higher loads will produce a more significant HR response than in previous phases.

**Flat dumbbell chest press** — 2 sets × 12 reps. Used as an accessory volume set after the incline press. Lighter load than the incline working sets.

**Push-up (full, from toes)** — 3 sets × maximum reps with continuous breathing, stopping 3 reps before failure. If the client cannot yet perform a full push-up with continuous breathing and controlled tempo, continue with incline push-ups. Do not sacrifice breathing quality for the full push-up position.

**Cable face pull** — already listed above — perform as the final upper body exercise to finish with a pulling movement and reinforce postural balance.

*Cool-down:* 5 minutes treadmill walk. Stretches: chest doorway stretch (60 seconds), lat stretch (45 seconds each side), posterior shoulder stretch (30 seconds each side), thoracic extension over foam roller (10 slow extensions).

---

**Session C — Cardiovascular Conditioning (Week 9)**

*Warm-up:* 5 minutes upright bike at light resistance.

*Main work — moderate intensity intervals (40 minutes total):*

This is the first session at Phase III cardiovascular intensity. The structure is a 2:1 work-to-recovery ratio at genuinely moderate intensity.

5 minutes steady walk at 4.0 km/h, flat (HR should reach approximately 100–105 bpm — this is the warm-up within the cardio session).

Then: **8 × (3 minutes at 5.0–5.5 km/h, 2–3% incline / target HR 122–128 bpm + 90 seconds at 3.5 km/h, flat / HR recovery to below 108 bpm)** = 36 minutes of interval work.

The work intervals are brisk walking with incline — not running. The combination of speed and incline produces the target HR without the joint impact of running, which is not appropriate for this client at this stage. Monitor HR at the end of every work interval. If HR exceeds 132 bpm during a work interval, reduce the incline immediately. If HR does not recover below 108 bpm during the recovery interval, extend the recovery to 2 minutes before the next work interval.

*Cool-down:* 5 minutes at 3.0 km/h, flat. Seated rest with HR monitoring for 5 minutes. Final HR should be below 95 bpm before the client leaves.

**Why this intensity matters:** Moderate-intensity interval training at 75–85% of maximum HR produces significantly greater improvements in VO2 max, endothelial function, and cardiac output than the steady-state work of Phases I and II. A landmark study by Wisløff et al. (2007) demonstrated that interval training at this intensity produced superior improvements in VO2 max, cardiac function, and quality of life compared to continuous moderate exercise in post-MI patients. This is the evidence base for the Phase III cardiovascular progression.

---

**Session D — Full Body Strength Circuit (Week 9)**

This session uses moderate loads at higher reps in a circuit format. It develops muscular endurance, cardiovascular fitness, and whole-body coordination simultaneously. The circuit format means rest periods are shorter than the dedicated strength sessions — HR will be higher throughout, typically sitting at 115–125 bpm during the working portions. This is now acceptable under Phase III parameters.

*Warm-up:* 10 minutes — 5 minutes recumbent bike, 5 minutes mobility.

*Circuit structure:* 3 rounds of the following circuit. Rest 60 seconds between exercises within the circuit. Rest 3 minutes between rounds. Check HR at the end of each exercise — if it exceeds 128 bpm, extend the rest before the next exercise.

**Exercise 1 — Goblet squat** — 15 reps. Moderate load (12–16 kg). Exhale on the stand.

**Exercise 2 — Dumbbell chest press (flat bench)** — 12 reps. Moderate load — lighter than Session B working sets. Exhale on the press.

**Exercise 3 — Dumbbell RDL** — 12 reps. Moderate load. Exhale on the return to standing.

**Exercise 4 — Seated cable row** — 15 reps. Moderate load — lighter than Session B working sets. Exhale on the pull.

**Exercise 5 — Step-up (25–30 cm step, light dumbbells)** — 10 reps each leg. Exhale on the step up.

**Exercise 6 — Dumbbell lateral raise** — 15 reps. Light load. Exhale on the raise.

**Exercise 7 — Pallof press** — 10 reps each side. Exhale on the press out.

**Exercise 8 — Farmer's carry** — 30 metres. Moderate dumbbells (12–14 kg each hand). Walk slowly and deliberately, tall posture. HR will rise during this — monitor on return.

*Cool-down:* 5 minutes slow treadmill walk. Full body stretching routine — 5 minutes.

### WEEK 10

**Theme:** Load progression on all primary compound movements. Introduce the barbell back squat. Extend cardiovascular interval duration.

---

**Session A — Lower Body Strength (Week 10)**

*Warm-up:* Same as Week 9 with the addition of 2 sets of 5 empty barbell squats (just the bar, 20 kg) to prepare for the barbell squat introduction.

*Primary compound movement:*

**Barbell back squat (low bar position)** — 4 sets × 6 reps. This is the most significant exercise introduction of the entire programme. Approach it with appropriate care.

**Setup and technique brief:** Use the low bar position — bar resting across the rear deltoids and upper trapezius, not on the neck. This position reduces the moment arm on the lower back compared to high bar and is generally more comfortable for older adults with limited thoracic mobility. Add load only if all three are satisfactory. A spotter or safety bars in a squat rack are mandatory. Never squat without safety equipment in place.

**HR note:** The barbell squat will produce a higher HR response than any previous lower body exercise. Check HR after every set. Rest 3 full minutes between sets. If HR exceeds 130 bpm after a set, extend rest to 4 minutes.

**Trap bar deadlift** — 3 sets × 6 reps. Load increase from Week 9. The rep range drops from 8 to 6, allowing a meaningful load increase. Rest 3 minutes.
