# Phase III Interval Conditioning Programme
### Complete Integration with Weeks 9–12 Strength and Nutrition Plan

---

## Clinical Framework for Interval Training Post-MI

The introduction of structured interval conditioning at Phase III clearance represents the most evidence-rich upgrade available to this client's programme. Before detailing the sessions, it is worth establishing the physiological rationale, the safety architecture, and the specific interval methodology that is appropriate for a post-MI patient at this stage of recovery — because interval training in cardiac rehabilitation is a nuanced topic that has been significantly misunderstood in both directions. Some trainers avoid it entirely out of excessive caution; others apply generic HIIT protocols without understanding the cardiac-specific considerations. Neither approach serves the client well.

### The Evidence Base

The landmark paper in this field is Wisløff et al. (2007), published in *Circulation*, which compared high-intensity interval training against moderate continuous exercise in post-MI patients and found that the interval group achieved a 46% improvement in VO2 max compared to 14% in the continuous group, alongside superior improvements in cardiac output, endothelial function, and quality of life. Subsequent meta-analyses — including Pattyn et al. (2014) and the SAINTEX-CAD trial — have consistently confirmed that interval training is not only safe in stable cardiac populations but produces superior cardiovascular adaptations compared to continuous moderate exercise alone.

Critically, the safety data is reassuring. A 2012 review by Rognmo et al. examining over 175,000 hours of high-intensity exercise in cardiac rehabilitation patients found the risk of fatal cardiac events during high-intensity exercise to be approximately 1 in 129,456 patient-hours — lower than many clinicians assume, and comparable to moderate-intensity exercise risk in the same population. The key word is *structured* — supervised, progressive, with appropriate monitoring and clear stopping criteria.

For this client specifically, the Phase III clearance to 85% of age-predicted maximum HR (136 bpm) means that genuine moderate-to-vigorous intensity intervals are now physiologically accessible and clinically sanctioned. The programme below uses a **moderate-intensity interval training (MIIT)** approach in Weeks 9–10, progressing to **vigorous-intensity interval training (VIIT)** in Weeks 11–12 — deliberately avoiding the term HIIT, which implies maximal or near-maximal effort that remains prohibited.

### Interval Intensity Definitions for This Client

Given the client's age-predicted maximum HR of 162 bpm and Phase III ceiling of 136 bpm, the working zones are defined as follows.

| Zone | Name | HR Range | % Max | RPE | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Recovery | <100 bpm | <62% | 9–10 | Active rest between intervals |
| 2 | Aerobic base | 100–112 bpm | 62–69% | 11–12 | Phase I–II steady state |
| 3 | Moderate intensity | 113–122 bpm | 70–75% | 12–13 | Phase III entry level |
| 4 | Vigorous intensity | 123–132 bpm | 76–82% | 13–15 | Phase III target work zone |
| 5 | Ceiling approach | 133–136 bpm | 82–85% | 15 | Hard ceiling — brief only |
| — | Hard stop | >136 bpm | >85% | — | Stop immediately |

Zone 4 is the primary target for work intervals in Phase III. Zone 3 is used for moderate intervals and as a transition zone. Zone 1 is the recovery target between intervals. Zone 5 is approached only briefly and incidentally — it is never a target.

### Modality Selection

Four cardiovascular modalities are used across the Phase III interval programme, each chosen for specific reasons.

**Treadmill walking with incline** is the primary modality for Weeks 9–10. Incline walking produces Zone 4 HR responses without the joint impact of running, which is not appropriate for a 58-year-old post-MI patient in the first weeks of Phase III. The incline can be adjusted in real time to manage HR, making it the most controllable modality.

**Upright stationary bike** is introduced as a primary interval modality from Week 10. Cycling is non-weight-bearing, eliminates fall risk, and allows very precise resistance adjustments. It is the modality used in the majority of cardiac rehabilitation interval research, including the Wisløff protocol.

**Rowing ergometer** is introduced in Week 11 as a supplementary modality. Rowing is a full-body cardiovascular exercise that engages the posterior chain, develops upper body endurance, and produces excellent cardiovascular stimulus. It requires careful technique instruction to avoid excessive lumbar flexion under fatigue. It is not used as a primary modality until the client has demonstrated consistent HR management on the treadmill and bike.

**Ski erg or cross-trainer (elliptical)** is introduced in Week 12 as a variety modality. The elliptical provides a low-impact, full-body cardiovascular stimulus that bridges the gap between cycling and running mechanics. The ski erg develops upper body cardiovascular endurance and posterior chain engagement in a way that no other modality replicates.

### Monitoring Protocol for Interval Sessions

The monitoring requirements for interval sessions are more demanding than for steady-state cardio or resistance training. The following protocol applies to every interval session in Phase III.

The client wears a chest-strap HR monitor throughout. You observe the HR display continuously during work intervals — not just at the end. HR during work intervals should be checked at the 60-second mark and the end of each interval. HR during recovery intervals should be checked at the 60-second mark to confirm it is trending downward. If HR does not return to Zone 1 (below 100 bpm) within the prescribed recovery period, extend the recovery before the next work interval. If HR fails to recover below 100 bpm after two consecutive extended recoveries, end the interval session and transition to 10 minutes of slow walking cool-down.

Blood pressure should be checked before every interval session. If resting systolic BP exceeds 160 mmHg or diastolic exceeds 100 mmHg, do not proceed with interval training that day — perform a steady-state Zone 2 session instead and flag the reading to the cardiologist.

Symptom screening before every session: ask the client directly about chest discomfort, unusual fatigue, dizziness, palpitations, or shortness of breath at rest in the preceding 24 hours. Any positive response warrants a conservative session or rest day and medical follow-up if symptoms are ongoing.

---

## Interval Session Architecture — Week by Week

The interval conditioning programme follows a deliberate progression across the four weeks of Phase III. Each week introduces one meaningful change — either increased work interval duration, increased intensity, decreased recovery ratio, or a new modality. Never change more than one variable in a single week.

---

## WEEK 9 — INTERVAL FOUNDATION

**Interval theme:** Establish the work-recovery pattern. Introduce Zone 4 HR in a controlled, brief format. Build confidence at the new intensity ceiling.

**Interval sessions this week:** Two dedicated interval sessions replace the single cardiovascular conditioning session from Phase II. This is the most significant structural change to the weekly programme. The four-session week now looks as follows.

- Session A: Lower body strength
- Session B: Interval conditioning 1 (treadmill incline)
- Session C: Upper body strength
- Session D: Interval conditioning 2 (bike) + full body circuit (abbreviated)

Note that Session D combines a shorter interval block with the full body circuit from the original programme. This is manageable in Week 9 because the interval block is brief and the circuit uses moderate loads. From Week 10, these are separated into distinct sessions, requiring a fifth session per week — discuss this with the client and confirm schedule availability.

---

### Session B — Interval Conditioning 1: Treadmill Incline (Week 9)

**Total session time:** 45 minutes
**Modality:** Treadmill
**Target work zone:** Zone 3–4 (113–128 bpm)
**Recovery zone:** Zone 1 (below 100 bpm)

*Warm-up (10 minutes):*

Begin with 3 minutes on the treadmill at 3.5 km/h, flat. This is not the cardiovascular warm-up — it is the locomotor warm-up, allowing the client to find their walking rhythm and posture before any intensity is applied. Follow with 2 minutes of dynamic mobility off the treadmill: 10 leg swings each direction (forward-back and side-to-side, holding the treadmill frame for balance), 10 hip circles each direction, 10 ankle circles each direction, 10 bodyweight calf raises. Return to the treadmill for 5 minutes at 4.0 km/h, flat — this is the aerobic warm-up, bringing HR to approximately 100–105 bpm before the intervals begin.

Check HR before starting the interval block. It should be between 95 and 108 bpm. If it is above 108 bpm, extend the flat walking warm-up by 3 minutes.

*Interval block (25 minutes):*

**Protocol: 6 × (2 minutes work + 2 minutes recovery) + 1 minute transition = 25 minutes**

This is a 1:1 work-to-recovery ratio with short work intervals. The short duration is deliberate — two minutes is long enough to drive HR into Zone 4 but short enough that the client does not sustain high cardiac demand for an extended period. As the weeks progress, work interval duration increases while recovery duration decreases, progressively challenging the cardiovascular system.

**Work interval parameters:** Speed 4.5–5.0 km/h, incline 4–6%. The combination of moderate speed and incline is what drives HR into Zone 4 without requiring running. Adjust the incline in real time based on HR response — if HR reaches 128 bpm before the 2 minutes is complete, reduce the incline by 1–2% immediately. The target is to spend the majority of the work interval between 118 and 128 bpm, not to hit the ceiling.

**Recovery interval parameters:** Speed 3.0 km/h, incline 0%. The client walks slowly on a flat surface. Target HR recovery to below 100 bpm within the 2-minute recovery window. If HR is still above 105 bpm at the end of the recovery interval, extend recovery by 60 seconds before the next work interval and note this in the session log — it indicates the work interval was too demanding and the incline should be reduced in the next interval.

**Interval-by-interval guidance:**

*Interval 1:* 4.5 km/h, 4% incline. This is the calibration interval. Watch HR closely. Note the time it takes to reach Zone 4. If HR reaches Zone 4 within 60 seconds, the incline is too high — reduce to 3% for Interval 2. If HR does not reach Zone 3 by the end of the 2 minutes, the incline is too low — increase to 5% for Interval 2.

*Interval 2:* Adjust based on Interval 1 data. Target HR 118–125 bpm by the 90-second mark.

*Intervals 3–4:* Maintain the calibrated speed and incline. HR will typically be slightly higher in intervals 3–4 than in intervals 1–2 due to cardiovascular drift — this is normal and expected. If HR exceeds 128 bpm, reduce incline by 1%.

*Intervals 5–6:* The client should now be well into the work-recovery rhythm. These final intervals are the most demanding due to cumulative fatigue. Maintain the same parameters as intervals 3–4. If the client reports RPE above 14 or HR exceeds 130 bpm, reduce the incline and complete the interval at the lower intensity rather than stopping — partial completion at reduced intensity is preferable to stopping entirely.

*Cool-down (10 minutes):*

5 minutes at 3.0 km/h, flat. HR should return to below 95 bpm within this period. If it does not, continue walking until it does — do not allow the client to sit down abruptly after interval work, as this can cause venous pooling and a sudden drop in cardiac preload. Follow with 5 minutes of seated stretching: calf stretch, hamstring stretch, hip flexor stretch. Final HR check — below 90 bpm before leaving the treadmill area.

**Session log entries:** Record for each interval — start HR, peak HR, end-of-interval HR, recovery HR at 60 seconds, recovery HR at 120 seconds, incline used, speed used, RPE. This data is invaluable for progression decisions in subsequent weeks.

---

### Session D — Interval Conditioning 2: Bike + Full Body Circuit (Week 9)

**Total session time:** 55 minutes
**Structure:** 20-minute bike interval block followed by 30-minute full body circuit (as per original programme) with 5-minute transition

*Bike interval block (20 minutes):*

**Warm-up within the block:** 5 minutes on the upright stationary bike at minimal resistance, cadence 70–80 rpm. HR should reach 95–105 bpm.

**Protocol: 5 × (90 seconds work + 90 seconds recovery)**

This is a shorter interval block than Session B, using the bike as the modality. The bike allows more precise resistance control than the treadmill and is the modality used in the majority of cardiac rehabilitation research.

**Work interval parameters:** Increase resistance to a level that drives HR to 120–128 bpm within 60–75 seconds. Maintain cadence at 75–85 rpm. The resistance level will need to be calibrated in the first interval — start conservatively and increase if HR does not reach Zone 4 by 75 seconds.

**Recovery interval parameters:** Drop resistance to minimal, cadence 60–70 rpm. Active recovery — do not stop pedalling. Target HR below 100 bpm by the end of the 90-second recovery. Active recovery (continuing to pedal at low intensity) is superior to passive recovery (stopping) for cardiac populations because it maintains venous return and prevents the abrupt haemodynamic changes associated with sudden cessation of exercise.

**Why 90-second intervals on the bike?** The bike produces a slightly faster HR response than treadmill walking because the smaller muscle mass of the legs working against resistance creates a higher relative cardiovascular demand per unit of work. Ninety-second work intervals are sufficient to drive meaningful cardiovascular adaptation without the extended high-HR exposure of the 2-minute treadmill intervals.

*Transition (5 minutes):*

Step off the bike. Walk slowly around the gym floor for 3 minutes — do not sit down. HR should be below 105 bpm before beginning the circuit. If it is not, extend the walk by 2 minutes.

*Full body circuit (30 minutes):*

As per the original programme Session D — 3 rounds of the circuit at moderate loads. Given that the client has already completed a cardiovascular interval block, reduce the circuit loads by approximately 10–15% compared to a standalone circuit session. The circuit HR will be higher than usual due to residual cardiovascular elevation — monitor carefully and extend rest between exercises if HR exceeds 125 bpm.

---

## WEEK 10 — INTERVAL PROGRESSION

**Interval theme:** Increase work interval duration. Introduce the bike as a standalone interval modality. Begin to reduce the work-to-recovery ratio from 1:1 toward 2:1.

**Weekly structure (five sessions):**

- Session A: Lower body strength
- Session B: Interval conditioning 1 (treadmill incline — extended intervals)
- Session C: Upper body strength
- Session D: Interval conditioning 2 (bike — standalone)
- Session E: Full body circuit (standalone, moderate)

The addition of a fifth session is a significant increase in weekly training volume. Confirm the client is recovering adequately — sleep quality, energy levels, muscle soreness, and resting HR (which should be stable or declining; a resting HR elevated by more than 5–7 bpm above baseline suggests inadequate recovery). If the client is not recovering well, keep Session E as active recovery rather than a circuit session for the first week of the five-session structure.

---

### Session B — Interval Conditioning 1: Treadmill Incline (Week 10)

**Total session time:** 48 minutes
**Protocol: 6 × (3 minutes work + 2 minutes recovery)**

Work interval duration increases from 2 minutes to 3 minutes. Recovery remains at 2 minutes. This shifts the work-to-recovery ratio from 1:1 to 3:2 — a meaningful progression in cardiovascular demand.

*Warm-up (10 minutes):* Same as Week 9.

*Interval block (30 minutes):*

**Work interval parameters:** Speed 4.5–5.0 km/h, incline 4–6% (calibrated from Week 9 session logs). The additional minute of work means HR will reach a higher peak than in Week 9 — expect peak HR to be 3–5 bpm higher than Week 9 peaks for equivalent incline and speed. If Week 9 peak HR was consistently at 125–128 bpm, reduce the incline by 1% in Week 10 to account for the longer work duration.

**Recovery interval parameters:** 3.0 km/h, flat, 2 minutes. The recovery window is unchanged at 2 minutes despite the longer work interval — this is the progression challenge. HR recovery may not be complete within 2 minutes in the early intervals of Week 10. This is acceptable as long as HR is trending clearly downward and reaches below 105 bpm by the end of the recovery window. If HR is above 108 bpm at the end of any recovery interval, extend recovery by 60 seconds.

**New addition — HR drift monitoring:** In Week 10, begin tracking cardiovascular drift explicitly. Record peak HR in each work interval. In a well-conditioned cardiovascular system, peak HR across intervals of equal intensity should be relatively stable or show only modest drift (2–4 bpm increase from interval 1 to interval 6). Significant drift (more than 8–10 bpm increase from first to last interval) indicates the work intensity is too high for the current fitness level and should be reduced.

*Cool-down (8 minutes):* 5 minutes slow treadmill walk, 3 minutes seated stretching.

---

### Session D — Interval Conditioning 2: Bike Standalone (Week 10)

**Total session time:** 45 minutes
**Protocol: 8 × (90 seconds work + 90 seconds recovery)**

Increase from 5 to 8 intervals. Total work time increases from 7.5 minutes to 12 minutes — a 60% increase in interval volume on the bike. This is the primary cardiovascular progression variable for the bike modality in Week 10.

*Warm-up (8 minutes):* 5 minutes easy cycling, 3 minutes dynamic mobility.

*Interval block (24 minutes):*

**Work interval parameters:** Same resistance as Week 9 calibrated level, or a small increase if Week 9 HR data showed consistent recovery and peak HR below 125 bpm. Cadence 80–90 rpm during work intervals — a higher cadence than Week 9, which increases cardiovascular demand without increasing resistance. This is an important distinction: increasing cadence at the same resistance is a lower-risk progression than increasing resistance, because the cardiovascular response is more gradual and more easily managed.

**Recovery interval parameters:** Minimal resistance, cadence 60 rpm, active recovery. Target HR below 100 bpm.

**Introduce perceived exertion anchoring:** From Week 10, ask the client to report RPE at the end of every work interval using the Borg 6–20 scale. Record this alongside HR. Over time, the relationship between RPE and HR at a given workload should shift — as fitness improves, the same RPE will correspond to a higher workload and a lower HR. This is one of the clearest markers of cardiovascular adaptation and is motivating for the client to observe.

*Cool-down (8 minutes):* 5 minutes easy cycling, 3 minutes seated stretching.

---

### Session E — Full Body Circuit (Week 10)

As per the original programme, standalone. Full loads as prescribed. This session is now separated from the interval block, allowing both to be performed at full capacity.

---

## WEEK 11 — VIGOROUS INTENSITY INTRODUCTION

**Interval theme:** Introduce vigorous-intensity intervals (Zone 4 upper range, 126–132 bpm). Introduce the rowing ergometer. Extend treadmill work intervals to 4 minutes. Reduce recovery ratio toward 2:1.

**Weekly structure:** Five sessions as per Week 10.

This is the most demanding week of the entire 12-week programme. Monitor recovery indicators closely. If the client shows signs of overreaching — elevated resting HR, poor sleep, unusual muscle soreness, low motivation, or any cardiac symptoms — reduce interval intensity immediately and consult the cardiologist if symptoms are present.

# Emergency Programme Modification
### Immediate Regression to Phase II Parameters

---

## Immediate Clinical Response

Stop. Before any programming discussion, this requires a clear clinical response protocol, and it needs to happen before the client returns to the gym.

**Chest tightness during exercise in a post-MI patient is a cardiac symptom until proven otherwise.** It does not matter that he has Phase III clearance. It does not matter that he has been progressing well. Chest tightness during exertion in this population has a defined differential diagnosis that includes exercise-induced angina, myocardial ischaemia, arrhythmia, and re-stenosis of a previously treated coronary artery — all of which require medical evaluation before any further exercise takes place.

### What You Must Do Right Now

**Step 1 — Document the episode precisely.** Write down everything you observed and everything the client reported while the details are fresh. Record the following: the exact time the tightness began, which interval number it occurred during, the speed and incline at the time, the client's HR at the time of symptom onset, how long the tightness lasted, whether it resolved with rest and how quickly, whether it radiated anywhere (jaw, arm, shoulder, back), whether it was accompanied by any other symptoms (breathlessness beyond expected exertion, dizziness, nausea, unusual sweating, palpitations), and the client's exact words describing the sensation. This documentation goes to the cardiologist.

**Step 2 — Contact the cardiologist today.** Not tomorrow. Not at the next scheduled appointment. Today. Provide the documented episode report. The cardiologist needs to decide whether this warrants urgent evaluation (same-day or next-day stress test, ECG, or cardiology review) or whether it can be assessed at a scheduled appointment. That decision belongs to the cardiologist, not to you. Your role is to communicate clearly and promptly.

**Step 3 — The client does not train again until medical clearance is received.** This is not a conservative suggestion — it is the only appropriate course of action. Exercise-induced chest tightness in a post-MI patient that has not been medically evaluated is an absolute contraindication to further exercise. There are no exceptions to this rule. If the client pushes back, explain clearly that your professional and ethical obligation is to his safety, and that returning to exercise without clearance exposes him to a risk that no training benefit can justify.

**Step 4 — When the cardiologist responds, obtain written or documented verbal clearance** specifying the parameters under which the client may return to exercise. Do not rely on the client's summary of a phone conversation with the cardiologist — speak directly with the medical team or obtain written documentation. The parameters in this revised programme are based on the assumption that the cardiologist clears the client for a return to supervised exercise at Phase II intensity. If the cardiologist specifies different parameters, those take absolute precedence over everything in this document.

**Step 5 — Review your emergency action plan.** If the chest tightness had been more severe, had not resolved with rest, or had been accompanied by additional symptoms, you would have called emergency services immediately. Revisit your gym's emergency action plan, confirm your AED location and your CPR certification is current, and ensure you have the client's cardiologist contact, GP contact, and next-of-kin contact readily accessible at every session.

---

## What This Symptom Means for the Programme

Assuming the cardiologist evaluates the client, identifies the cause of the chest tightness, and clears him to return to supervised exercise at Phase II parameters, the programme below applies. The revised programme is built on the following clinical reasoning.

The chest tightness occurred during vigorous-intensity interval work — specifically during the Phase III interval sessions that were pushing HR to 122–132 bpm. The most likely exercise-related explanation is that the cardiovascular demand of those sessions exceeded what the myocardium could safely sustain at this point in recovery, either because the progression was too aggressive, because an underlying issue was not fully resolved, or because an external factor (medication timing, hydration, sleep, emotional stress, a concurrent illness) lowered the threshold for symptom onset. The cardiologist's evaluation will clarify which of these is the case.

Regardless of the specific cause, the appropriate response is the same: return to a level of exercise intensity that is well within the client's demonstrated safe range, rebuild confidence and physiological tolerance gradually, and progress far more conservatively than the Phase III programme did. The Phase II parameters — HR ceiling 115 bpm, no Valsalva, RPE ceiling 13, no maximal effort — provided a safe and productive training environment for eight weeks without incident. That is the environment we return to.

This is not a failure. It is the programme working as it should — the monitoring systems detected a symptom, the appropriate response is being implemented, and the client will return to training in a safer and more carefully managed context. Frame this for the client in exactly those terms.

---

## Psychological Considerations

A cardiac symptom during exercise is frightening. For a patient who is six months post-MI and has been working hard to rebuild his fitness and confidence, experiencing chest tightness during a training session may trigger significant anxiety, fear of exercise, and loss of confidence in his body. These psychological responses are entirely normal and must be addressed directly.

When the client returns to training, spend the first session — and several sessions thereafter — explicitly acknowledging how he is feeling. Ask open questions: how is he feeling about being back in the gym, does he feel anxious during exercise, is he monitoring his body more than usual? Validate whatever he reports. Reassure him that the programme has been restructured specifically to keep him well within safe limits, that you are monitoring his HR continuously, and that the goal right now is to rebuild trust — his trust in his body, and his body's trust in the exercise stimulus.

Consider recommending that he speak with his GP about the psychological impact of the episode if anxiety is significant. Cardiac anxiety — sometimes called cardiophobia — is a recognised and treatable condition that affects a meaningful proportion of post-MI patients and can significantly impair rehabilitation outcomes if left unaddressed.

Do not rush the return to higher intensities. The client's psychological readiness to exercise at moderate intensity is as important as his physiological readiness. If he is anxious and hypervigilant during sessions, his sympathetic nervous system activation will elevate HR and blood pressure independently of the exercise stimulus, making HR-based monitoring less reliable and the exercise experience more stressful. Patience here is not just compassionate — it is clinically appropriate.

---

## Revised Programme Parameters — Phase II Return

### Hard Limits (Reinstated)

Every parameter returns to Phase II standards. These are not suggestions — they are the governing rules of every session until the cardiologist explicitly upgrades them again.

**Heart rate ceiling: 115 bpm.** This is a hard stop. If HR reaches 115 bpm during any activity, the client stops, sits, and rests until HR returns below 100 bpm. You record the context — what exercise, what load, what set number, what time into the session. This data goes to the cardiologist at the next review.

**No Valsalva manoeuvre of any kind.** The modified Valsalva permitted under Phase III clearance is withdrawn entirely. Continuous breathing on every exercise, every rep, every set. Exhale on the effort, inhale on the return. This is cued verbally on every set for as long as necessary.

**RPE ceiling: 13/20.** Somewhat hard is the absolute maximum. Most working sets should feel like 11–12. If the client reports RPE above 13 at any point, reduce the load or intensity immediately.

**Minimum reps in reserve: 4.** No set should approach failure. The client should always feel he could comfortably perform four or more additional reps at the end of every working set.

**No interval training.** All cardiovascular work returns to continuous steady-state exercise at Zone 2–3 intensity (100–112 bpm). Interval training is suspended entirely until the cardiologist re-evaluates and provides explicit clearance for it. When interval training does eventually return — if it does — it will begin at a far more conservative entry point than the Phase III programme used.

**Session duration cap: 45 minutes of active work.** Total session time including warm-up and cool-down should not exceed 60 minutes. This is a reduction from the Phase III sessions, which were running to 50–55 minutes of active work.

**Session frequency: Three sessions per week maximum.** The five-session Phase III structure is suspended. Three sessions per week with at least one full rest day between each session. This reduces cumulative cardiovascular load and provides adequate recovery time.

**Mandatory rest day before and after the first return session.** The client's first session back should be preceded by a full rest day and followed by a full rest day. Do not schedule the return session on a Monday if the client trained on Friday.

## Return-to-Exercise Protocol

### Before the First Session Back

Obtain written or documented clearance from the cardiologist. Review the clearance parameters with the client in person before he changes into his gym kit — not during the warm-up, not between sets. Sit down, go through the revised programme, explain what has changed and why, and answer his questions. This conversation should take 15–20 minutes and is as important as any training session.

Check resting HR and blood pressure before every session from this point forward. Record both values. If resting HR is more than 10 bpm above the client's established baseline, or if systolic BP exceeds 150 mmHg, do not train that day. Rest and reassess the following day. If elevated readings persist for more than two consecutive days, contact the cardiologist.

Establish a symptom check-in at the start of every session. Ask the client directly: any chest discomfort, tightness, pressure, or pain since the last session? Any unusual breathlessness at rest or with light activity? Any palpitations or irregular heartbeat sensations? Any dizziness or lightheadedness? Any unusual fatigue? A positive answer to any of these questions means no training that day and a call to the cardiologist.

### The First Session Back — Structure

The first session back is not a training session in the conventional sense. It is a reassurance session. The goals are to confirm that the client can exercise at low intensity without symptoms, to rebuild his confidence in the gym environment, and to establish the new baseline from which the revised programme will progress.

**First session structure:**

Arrive at the gym and sit together for 5 minutes. Check resting HR and BP. Ask the symptom screening questions. If all clear, proceed.

Ten minutes on the recumbent bike at the absolute lowest resistance. HR target: 90–100 bpm. RPE: 9–10. The client should feel almost nothing — this is deliberately easy. Talk to him throughout. Monitor HR continuously. If HR exceeds 105 bpm at any point, reduce resistance further.

If the recumbent bike is well tolerated after 10 minutes, perform 15 minutes of very light resistance work — two exercises only. Seated leg press at a load well below his Phase II working weight (approximately 50% of his last Phase II working load), two sets of 12 reps. Seated cable row at the same relative load, two sets of 12 reps. Check HR after every set. Continuous breathing cued on every rep.

Five minutes slow walking on the treadmill at 2.5 km/h, flat. HR should be below 95 bpm throughout.

Five minutes seated rest with HR monitoring.

Total session: approximately 35 minutes. If the client is symptom-free throughout and HR stayed below 110 bpm, the session is a success. Document everything.

# Phase II Safe Activity Framework
### What the Client Can Do Right Now

---

## The Governing Principle

Before listing activities, establish the right mental model for this period. The question is not simply what exercises are technically permissible under Phase II parameters — it is what activities will maintain the client's physical condition, protect his cardiovascular health, support his psychological wellbeing, and keep him engaged with the process while the medical picture is clarified.

This period has three concurrent goals that must be held simultaneously.

**Maintain what has been built.** Eight weeks of consistent training have produced real adaptations — improved cardiovascular efficiency, increased muscle mass and strength, better movement quality, and established habits. Most of these adaptations will be substantially preserved for four to six weeks of reduced intensity training before meaningful detraining begins. The Phase II return programme is not starting from scratch — it is holding ground while the situation is assessed.

**Do no harm.** Every activity choice must be filtered through the question of whether it could reproduce the chest tightness symptom. If there is any doubt, the answer is no. The chest tightness episode has reset the risk calculus. Activities that were appropriate at Phase III are not appropriate now, and some activities that were appropriate at late Phase II need to be reintroduced cautiously rather than assumed safe.

**Keep the client moving and engaged.** Complete rest is not the answer and is not what the cardiologist has prescribed. Appropriate physical activity at Phase II intensity is safe, beneficial, and important for the client's psychological recovery from the symptom episode. Inactivity carries its own cardiovascular risk and will accelerate the deconditioning the programme has been working to reverse.

---

## What Is Definitively Safe Right Now

The following activities are safe within Phase II parameters, meaning they can be performed with high confidence that they will not reproduce the chest tightness symptom, provided the HR ceiling of 115 bpm and RPE ceiling of 13 are respected throughout.

---

### In the Gym — Cardiovascular

**Recumbent bike** is the safest cardiovascular modality available and should be the primary cardiovascular tool during this period. The supported recumbent position reduces cardiac preload compared to upright exercise, the resistance is precisely controllable in real time, and the HR response is predictable and gradual. Target HR 100–110 bpm. Duration 20–30 minutes of continuous steady-state work. No intervals. No resistance increases that push HR above 110 bpm. This is the one cardiovascular modality that can be used with full confidence right now.

**Slow treadmill walking, flat** is safe as a secondary cardiovascular modality and as a warm-up and cool-down tool. Speed 3.0–3.5 km/h, zero incline. At this speed and grade, HR should sit comfortably between 90 and 105 bpm for most clients. Do not introduce incline — incline was a component of the interval sessions that produced the chest tightness, and while the incline itself is unlikely to be the causative factor, removing it eliminates one variable and keeps the cardiovascular demand clearly within safe limits. Duration up to 20 minutes.

**Upright stationary bike** can be used cautiously as a third option, but only after the recumbent bike has been well tolerated for at least two sessions in the return week. The upright position increases cardiac demand slightly compared to the recumbent. Keep resistance low, cadence 70–80 rpm, HR target 100–108 bpm, duration 15–20 minutes maximum. If HR approaches 110 bpm at any resistance level, return to the recumbent bike.

---

### In the Gym — Resistance Training

The following resistance exercises are safe within Phase II parameters. They are characterised by predictable HR responses, low spinal loading, supported positions where appropriate, and clear breathing cue opportunities. All are performed with continuous breathing — no Valsalva of any kind.

**Seated leg press** remains the anchor lower body strength exercise. It is safe because the client is fully supported, the load is precisely controlled, and the movement pattern is simple and well-established. Loads at 65–75% of Phase II working weight. Three sets of 12 reps. Rest 2 minutes between sets. HR check after every set.

**Seated cable row** remains the anchor upper body pulling exercise. Pulling movements are consistently lower HR than pressing movements at equivalent effort levels and are the most important exercises for the postural correction this client needs. Loads at 65–75% of Phase II working weight. Three sets of 12 reps. Rest 2 minutes.

**Lat pulldown** is safe and valuable. Same loading and set-rep parameters as the cable row. Alternate grip variations — wide overhand, close neutral — to maintain variety and target slightly different portions of the back musculature.

**Goblet squat to a high box** is safe as a movement quality exercise with light load. The box provides a safety net that limits depth and reduces the cardiovascular demand of the movement. Use 6–10 kg. Two to three sets of 10 reps. The free-standing goblet squat without a box is also safe at this load — the box is a psychological and physical safety measure rather than a strict necessity, but keep it in place this week.

**Glute bridge (bilateral, floor)** is one of the safest and most valuable exercises available right now. It is performed lying on the floor, produces a very low HR response, activates the posterior chain effectively, and requires no equipment. Three sets of 15 reps. Can be performed at the beginning of a session as part of the warm-up or as a working exercise. Progress to single-leg when bilateral is well established.

**Seated leg curl** is safe. Isolated hamstring work in a supported seated position produces a modest HR response and is appropriate throughout this period. Two to three sets of 12 reps at moderate load.

**Seated calf raise** is safe and specifically valuable for this client because it promotes venous return from the lower limbs — an important circulatory consideration post-MI. Two sets of 20 reps, full range of motion. Can be performed with a light plate on the thighs for modest resistance.

**Chest press machine** is safe as a pressing exercise during this period. The machine is preferred over dumbbells right now because it eliminates the stabilisation demand and produces a more predictable, lower HR response than free weights at equivalent loads. Two to three sets of 12 reps at light to moderate load. Exhale on every press.

**Dumbbell shoulder press (seated, light)** is safe with conservative loading. Keep the load at or below Phase I working weights for now — overhead pressing produces a higher HR response than most other upper body movements and warrants extra caution during this period. Two sets of 12 reps. If HR approaches 110 bpm after a set, reduce the load.

**Incline push-up (hands on bench)** is safe and maintains upper body pressing capacity without the cardiovascular demand of a loaded dumbbell press. Two sets of 10 reps with continuous breathing. This is a useful exercise precisely because the load is fixed at a fraction of bodyweight and cannot be accidentally increased.

**Band pull-apart** is safe in every session. It produces a negligible HR response, directly addresses the postural issues common in post-MI patients, and reinforces the shoulder health work that has been built over the programme. Three sets of 15 reps with a light band. Include this in every upper body session and consider adding it to lower body sessions as a filler exercise during rest periods.

**Dead bug** is the core exercise of choice during this period. It is performed lying on the floor, produces a very low HR response, requires continuous breathing by its nature, and develops the deep abdominal stabilisers without any spinal loading. Three sets of 8–10 reps each side. This should appear in every session.

**Pallof press (light cable load)** is safe as an anti-rotation core exercise. It is performed standing, which produces a slightly higher HR response than floor-based core work, but at light cable loads the response is modest and well within Phase II limits. Two sets of 10 reps each side.

**Farmer's carry (light dumbbells, short distance)** is safe at conservative loads — 8–10 kg per hand, 20 metres maximum. Walk slowly and deliberately. Monitor HR on return — it will be higher than expected relative to the apparent effort. Rest fully before the next carry. This exercise maintains grip strength, core stability, and functional capacity simultaneously.

---

### Outside the Gym — Daily Life Activity

This is an important category that is often overlooked in formal programme design but is highly relevant for a post-MI patient in a Phase II return period. The activities of daily life represent a significant proportion of total physical activity and have meaningful cardiovascular effects.

**Walking outdoors** is safe and should be actively encouraged. Flat terrain, comfortable pace, duration 20–30 minutes. The client should be able to hold a conversation throughout — if he cannot, he is walking too fast. Walking outdoors has additional benefits beyond the cardiovascular stimulus: exposure to natural light supports circadian rhythm and sleep quality, the psychological benefits of being outdoors are well-documented, and the social dimension of walking with a partner or friend provides motivation and accountability. Recommend daily walks on non-gym days.

**Gentle gardening** is safe provided it does not involve sustained heavy lifting, prolonged overhead work, or activities that cause breath-holding. Light weeding, watering, gentle digging with a small spade — these are appropriate. Moving heavy pots, sustained digging with a full-size spade, or carrying heavy loads of soil or compost are not appropriate during this period.

**Household activities** at a light to moderate level are safe. Cooking, light cleaning, slow stair climbing, gentle tidying. Activities that involve sustained effort, heavy lifting, or anything that causes the client to hold his breath are not appropriate.

**Swimming (gentle)** warrants a specific discussion with the cardiologist before being recommended. Swimming is an excellent cardiovascular modality for cardiac patients in general, but the prone position, the breath-holding associated with some swimming styles, the hydrostatic pressure on the chest, and the difficulty of monitoring HR in the water make it a modality that requires explicit medical clearance rather than assumption of safety. If the cardiologist clears it, gentle breaststroke or backstroke at a very easy pace is appropriate. Front crawl with bilateral breathing is not appropriate during this period.

**Sexual activity** is a question many post-MI patients have but few ask directly. The energy expenditure of sexual activity is roughly equivalent to climbing two flights of stairs or walking briskly — well within Phase II parameters for most patients. If the client raises this, the appropriate response is to confirm that it is generally safe at Phase II clearance level, to recommend he discuss it with his cardiologist if he has specific concerns, and to note that any chest tightness, breathlessness, or palpitations during sexual activity should be reported to the cardiologist immediately.

---

## What Is Not Safe Right Now

Being explicit about what to avoid is as important as listing what is safe. The following activities are suspended until the cardiologist re-evaluates and provides updated clearance.

**All interval training** of any kind is suspended. This includes the treadmill incline intervals, the bike intervals, the rowing intervals, and the full body circuit in its Phase III format. The chest tightness occurred during interval work. Until the cardiologist has identified why and confirmed it is safe to return to elevated HR exercise, intervals are off the table entirely. This is not a temporary inconvenience — it is the most important safety measure in the revised programme.

**Incline treadmill walking** is suspended. Even at low speeds, incline walking was a component of the interval sessions and produces a meaningfully higher cardiovascular demand than flat walking. Remove it entirely for now.

**The upright rowing ergometer** is suspended. Rowing produces a high cardiovascular demand relative to perceived effort, involves a complex breathing pattern that is difficult to maintain under fatigue, and was being introduced as a new modality at the time of the symptom episode. It is not appropriate during the Phase II return period.

**Free barbell exercises** — the barbell back squat and any other barbell movements introduced in Phase III — are suspended. These were introduced specifically because the modified Valsalva was permitted under Phase III clearance. With Valsalva withdrawn, the safety rationale for barbell loading is removed. Return to dumbbell and machine-based resistance work.

**The trap bar deadlift** is suspended for the same reason. It was introduced as a Phase III exercise with moderate Valsalva permitted. Without that clearance, the loading that makes it a meaningful strength stimulus is not appropriate. The dumbbell RDL can be reintroduced cautiously in Week 11 at conservative loads with continuous breathing.

**The Bulgarian split squat** is suspended. It produces a higher HR response than bilateral lower body exercises and was introduced as a Phase III progression. It is not appropriate during the Phase II return period.

**Any exercise that caused HR to approach or exceed 115 bpm** in previous sessions is suspended, regardless of whether it appears on the safe list above. The session logs from Phase II and Phase III contain HR data for every exercise — review them and identify any exercises that consistently drove HR above 110 bpm. Those exercises are suspended or performed at significantly reduced loads during this period.

**Group fitness classes** of any kind are not appropriate. The client cannot control the intensity of a group class, the instructor cannot monitor his HR individually, and the social pressure of a group environment may cause him to push beyond safe limits. This includes yoga classes that involve sustained holds, spin classes, circuit classes, and any other group format.

**Running or jogging** is not appropriate. It was not part of the programme at any stage and remains inappropriate for this client at this point in his recovery.

**Heavy manual work** — moving furniture, carrying heavy shopping, lifting anything that causes breath-holding — is not appropriate. If the client has tasks of this nature at home or work, they should be delegated or deferred until medical clearance is updated.

---

## Monitoring During This Period

The monitoring requirements during the Phase II return period are more stringent than during the original Phase II programme, because the chest tightness episode means the client's symptom threshold is now a known variable that must be tracked carefully.

**Every session:** Resting HR and BP before starting. Symptom screening questions before starting. HR check after every working set and every 3 minutes during cardiovascular work. RPE check at the end of every working set. Session log completed in full.

**Between sessions:** Ask the client to note any symptoms between sessions — chest discomfort at rest, unusual breathlessness, palpitations, dizziness, or fatigue that seems disproportionate to activity. Provide him with a simple symptom diary — a notes page on his phone is sufficient — and review it at the start of every session.

**Weekly:** Review the full session log. Calculate average peak HR per session and compare across weeks. Average peak HR should be stable or declining as fitness adapts to the Phase II stimulus. A rising average peak HR at constant load is a warning sign that warrants conservative management and possible medical review.

**Resting HR trend:** Encourage the client to check his resting HR first thing in the morning before getting out of bed, using his chest-strap monitor or a validated wrist device. Record it daily. A resting HR that is consistently 5–7 bpm above his established baseline for more than two consecutive days is a signal to rest and contact the cardiologist if it persists.

---

## What to Tell the Client

Frame this period clearly and honestly. He needs to understand why the restrictions are in place, what the plan is, and what success looks like right now — because without that framing, the regression to Phase II may feel like failure, and that psychological response will undermine his engagement with the programme.

Tell him the following, in your own words.

What happened during that interval session was his body sending a signal that the demand was too high at that moment. That signal was important and it was caught. The programme is designed to catch exactly that kind of signal, and the response — pulling back, getting medical evaluation, rebuilding carefully — is the programme working correctly. This is not a setback in the sense of losing ground permanently. It is a recalibration.

The work he has done over the past eight weeks has not disappeared. The cardiovascular adaptations, the strength gains, the movement quality, the habits — these are real and they are preserved. The Phase II return programme is not starting over. It is holding what has been built while the medical picture is clarified.

The goal right now is simple: complete every session without symptoms, keep HR below 115 bpm, and give the cardiologist the information they need to make a good decision about the next step. Every symptom-free session is a data point that supports a return to higher intensity work in the future. Every session where he pushes too hard and produces symptoms is a data point that delays that return.

His job right now is to be patient and consistent. Your job is to make sure every session is safe, productive, and as positive an experience as possible.

# CLINICAL PREAMBLE

## Patient Profile and Governing Parameters

**Client:** Male, 58 years old
**Status:** Six months post-myocardial infarction
**Initial clearance:** Phase II cardiac rehabilitation
**Phase III clearance:** Granted at Week 8 transition
**Phase III regression:** Implemented mid-Week 8 following chest tightness during interval training
**Current status:** Phase II parameters reinstated pending cardiologist re-evaluation

## Medication Considerations

Before implementing any component of this programme, confirm the client's full medication list with his cardiologist. The following interactions are clinically relevant and must be understood before training begins.

Beta-blockers blunt the heart rate response to exercise. If the client is taking metoprolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol, or any other beta-blocker, the age-predicted maximum HR of 162 bpm and all derived ceiling values will be artificially suppressed. In this case, RPE becomes the primary intensity guide and HR the secondary guide, rather than the reverse. Confirm with the cardiologist whether the HR ceilings in this programme require adjustment for beta-blocker effect.

Statins interact with grapefruit and grapefruit juice through CYP3A4 inhibition. Grapefruit is eliminated from the nutrition plan entirely.

Warfarin or other anticoagulants interact with vitamin K. If the client is on warfarin, leafy green vegetable intake must remain consistent day to day — do not dramatically increase or decrease consumption, as this destabilises INR. Do not recommend vitamin K supplementation.

ACE inhibitors and potassium-sparing diuretics can cause potassium retention. High-potassium dietary recommendations require confirmation with the prescribing physician before implementation.

## Universal Monitoring Protocol

The following monitoring requirements apply to every session throughout the entire 12-week programme regardless of phase.

The client wears a chest-strap HR monitor throughout every session. Wrist-based optical sensors are insufficiently accurate for this population and are not acceptable substitutes. HR is checked after every working set during resistance training and every three minutes during cardiovascular work. All readings are recorded in the session log.

Resting HR and blood pressure are checked before every session. If resting systolic BP exceeds 160 mmHg or diastolic exceeds 100 mmHg, the session does not proceed. The client rests, the reading is recorded, and the cardiologist is contacted if elevated readings persist across two consecutive days.

Symptom screening is conducted verbally before every session. Ask the client directly about chest discomfort, tightness, pressure, or pain since the last session; unusual breathlessness at rest or with light activity; palpitations or irregular heartbeat sensations; dizziness or lightheadedness; and unusual fatigue disproportionate to recent activity. Any positive response means no training that day. If symptoms are ongoing or worsening, contact the cardiologist.

## Emergency Action Protocol

Stop immediately and call emergency services if the client experiences chest pain or pressure of any kind during exercise, jaw or left arm pain or discomfort, severe breathlessness beyond expected exertion, dizziness or pre-syncope, syncope, palpitations or irregular heartbeat, or unusual pallor and sweating. Do not wait to see if symptoms resolve. Do not drive the client to hospital. Call emergency services, keep the client still and seated or lying down depending on symptoms, retrieve the AED, and begin CPR if the client loses consciousness and is not breathing normally. Your CPR certification must be current. The AED location must be known before every session begins.

## Breathing Protocol

Because Valsalva is prohibited in Phases I, II, and the Phase II return period, every resistance exercise uses continuous breathing throughout. Exhale on the concentric phase (the effort — the press, the pull, the stand, the drive). Inhale on the eccentric phase (the return — the lower, the release, the sit). Cue this verbally on every set for the first four weeks and whenever lapses are observed thereafter. In Phase III only, a brief moderate intra-abdominal brace of one to two seconds is permitted at the sticking point of moderate-load compound lifts, followed immediately by a controlled exhale. This is withdrawn entirely during the Phase II return period.

## Baseline Assessments (Week 0)

Complete the following before Week 1 begins. Results establish the baseline against which progress is measured at Weeks 4, 8, and 12.

Six-Minute Walk Test: record total distance covered and HR response throughout. Note the HR at the end of each minute and the peak HR achieved.

Thirty-second chair stand test: count the number of times the client can stand from a standard chair and return to seated in 30 seconds without using his arms.

Grip strength: measure with a hand dynamometer, three trials each hand, record the best result for each.

Resting HR and blood pressure: measure after five minutes of seated rest.

Movement screen: observe the squat pattern, hip hinge pattern, overhead reach, and single-leg balance. Note any limitations, asymmetries, or compensations.

# NUTRITION PLAN — CARDIAC HEALTH FOCUS

## Governing Principles

The nutrition plan operates throughout all 12 weeks and is adjusted by phase to reflect changing training demands. It is designed to complement medical dietary advice, not replace it. A referral to a registered dietitian with cardiovascular specialism is strongly recommended alongside this plan.

## Caloric Framework

Using the Mifflin-St Jeor equation for a 58-year-old male at approximately 82 kg and 175 cm:

Resting Metabolic Rate: (10 × 82) + (6.25 × 175) − (5 × 58) + 5 = approximately 1,629 kcal per day.

Activity multiplier of 1.4 in Phases I and II gives approximately 2,280 kcal per day. Activity multiplier of 1.55 in Phase III gives approximately 2,525 kcal per day. During the Phase II return period, return to the 1.4 multiplier — approximately 2,280 kcal per day. Adjust all values for the client's actual body weight.

If weight loss is a secondary goal confirmed by the cardiologist, apply a modest deficit of 200–300 kcal per day through food quality and composition rather than severe restriction.

## Macronutrient Targets

**Protein:** 1.4–1.6 g per kilogram of body weight per day. For an 82 kg client, this means 115–131 g of protein daily. Distribute across at least four eating occasions with 25–35 g per meal. Older adults experience anabolic resistance and require more dietary protein per kilogram than younger adults to achieve equivalent muscle protein synthesis.

Preferred sources: oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines, trout), skinless poultry, eggs, legumes (lentils, chickpeas, black beans, kidney beans), low-fat Greek yoghurt, cottage cheese, tofu, tempeh, edamame.

Sources to minimise: processed red meat (bacon, sausages, salami, deli meats) is largely eliminated. Unprocessed red meat is limited to 350–500 g cooked weight per week maximum.

**Carbohydrates:** 45–55% of total calories from carbohydrate, emphasising low-glycaemic, high-fibre sources. For a 2,200 kcal diet, approximately 248–303 g per day.

Preferred sources: rolled oats (75 g dry daily provides 3 g of beta-glucan for LDL reduction), sweet potato, new potatoes with skin, brown rice, quinoa, barley, wholegrain bread, berries, all vegetables.

Sources to minimise: white bread, white rice, refined pasta in large quantities, sugary drinks including fruit juice, pastries, biscuits, confectionery, ultra-processed foods.

Peri-workout strategy: a small carbohydrate and protein snack 60–90 minutes before training on training days. A banana with nut butter, or a small bowl of porridge. Post-session, a carbohydrate and protein combination within 30–60 minutes — Greek yoghurt with berries, or a wholegrain wrap with chicken and salad.

**Fats:** 30–35% of total calories from fat, strongly emphasising unsaturated fats. For a 2,200 kcal diet, approximately 73–86 g per day.

Preferred sources: extra-virgin olive oil as the primary cooking and dressing fat (2–4 tablespoons daily), oily fish three to four times per week for EPA and DHA omega-3 fatty acids, a 30 g handful of mixed nuts daily (walnuts, almonds, pistachios), avocado, ground flaxseed, chia seeds, hemp seeds.

Saturated fat: below 7% of total calories, approximately 17 g per day. Reduce fatty red meat, butter, cream, full-fat cheese, coconut oil, palm oil.

Trans fats: eliminated entirely. Avoid any product listing partially hydrogenated oil in the ingredients.

## The Five Cardiac Nutrition Pillars

**Pillar 1 — Mediterranean pattern as the overarching framework.** Abundant vegetables and fruit, legumes as a protein staple, whole grains, olive oil as the primary fat, regular oily fish, moderate poultry and eggs, limited red meat, minimal processed foods. Alcohol: discuss with the cardiologist. Current guidance does not recommend alcohol for cardiovascular benefit. Strict moderation or abstinence is the conservative position.

**Pillar 2 — Sodium management.** Target no more than 2,000 mg of sodium per day. Cook from scratch where possible. Use herbs, spices, lemon juice, and vinegar instead of salt. Choose tinned fish and vegetables in no-added-salt varieties. Read labels — above 0.6 g of salt per 100 g is considered high.

**Pillar 3 — Dietary fibre.** Target 30–35 g per day. Soluble fibre from oats, barley, legumes, apples, and psyllium husk binds bile acids and lowers LDL. Increase fibre gradually over two to three weeks if the client is currently eating a low-fibre diet. Increase water intake alongside fibre increases.

**Pillar 4 — Plant sterols and stanols.** 2 g per day from fortified foods (Flora ProActiv, Benecol, fortified yoghurt drinks) can reduce LDL by 10–15% when consumed consistently with meals. Discuss with the cardiologist before implementing.

**Pillar 5 — Hydration.** 2.0–2.5 litres of fluid per day, increasing to 2.5–3.0 litres on training days. Water is the primary fluid. Unsweetened herbal teas and green tea are appropriate alternatives. Caffeine up to 300–400 mg per day is generally safe but confirm with the cardiologist.

## Phase-Specific Nutrition Adjustments

**Phases I and II (Weeks 1–8):** Working caloric target 2,100–2,300 kcal per day. Focus on eliminating processed meats, sugary drinks, and trans fats in Week 1. Build the breakfast habit around porridge with berries, ground flaxseed, and walnuts. Introduce oily fish three times per week from Week 1. Introduce legumes as a daily staple from Week 5. Optimise post-session recovery nutrition from Week 5 — protein and carbohydrate within 30 minutes of resistance sessions.

**Phase III (Weeks 8–9 partial):** Increase daily caloric intake by 150–200 kcal on training days to support higher training volume. Add one extra serving of complex carbohydrate pre- or post-training. Maintain protein at 1.6 g per kilogram. Ensure pre-training meal of carbohydrate and protein 90–120 minutes before training. Discuss creatine monohydrate (3–5 g per day) with the cardiologist — growing evidence base for cardiovascular safety and potential benefit for increased strength training demands.

**Phase II Return (Weeks 9–12):** Return to Phase I and II caloric targets — 2,100–2,300 kcal per day. Maintain all dietary quality standards. Emphasise anti-inflammatory foods during this period: increase omega-3 rich fish, berries, leafy greens, turmeric, and ginger. Reduce any dietary stressors — excessive caffeine, alcohol if present, high-sodium convenience foods — that may contribute to cardiovascular reactivity. Ensure the client is eating adequately before sessions — hypoglycaemia during exercise is a cardiovascular stressor that must be avoided.

## Weeks 1–4

**Phase goals:** Establish safe HR response to exercise. Build movement competency. Develop the continuous breathing habit as automatic. Create a positive psychological relationship with the gym environment post-cardiac event. Establish baseline fitness metrics.

**Resistance parameters:** 2–3 sets | 12–15 reps | RPE 10–12 | Minimum 4 reps in reserve | Rest 90–120 seconds between sets | Tempo: 2 seconds eccentric, 1 second pause, 1–2 seconds concentric.

**Cardiovascular parameters:** Continuous steady-state only. HR target 95–108 bpm. RPE 10–11. Recumbent bike is the primary modality.

**Sessions per week:** Three. Minimum one full rest day between each session.

## WEEK 1

### Session 1 — Lower Body and Core Focus

**Warm-up (10 minutes)**

Five minutes on the recumbent bike at minimal resistance. HR should reach 85–95 bpm. Follow with five minutes of mobility: 10 seated thoracic rotations each side (sit tall, arms crossed over chest, rotate slowly), 10 ankle circles each direction, 10 glute bridges on the floor (feet flat, drive hips to ceiling, squeeze glutes at the top, lower with control — exhale on the drive up), 10 hip circles each direction.

Check HR before proceeding to working sets. It should be below 95 bpm.

**Working sets**

*Seated leg press — 2 sets × 15 reps.*
Feet hip-width apart on the platform, toes slightly out. Press through the whole foot — do not rise onto the toes. Do not lock the knees at the top. Lower under control for 2 seconds. Exhale on the press, inhale on the lower. Load: start conservatively — the client should feel the effort but be nowhere near failure. Check HR after each set. Rest 2 minutes.

*Glute bridge (floor, bilateral) — 2 sets × 15 reps.*
Lie on the floor, knees bent, feet flat. Drive the hips to the ceiling by squeezing the glutes. Hold 1 second at the top. Lower with control. Exhale on the drive up. Bodyweight only. Rest 60 seconds.

*Goblet squat to high box — 2 sets × 12 reps.*
Box height at chair level. Light dumbbell (4–6 kg) or bodyweight. Feet hip-width apart, toes out 15–30 degrees. Sit back to the box, stand tall. Exhale on the stand. Rest 90 seconds.

*Seated leg curl — 2 sets × 15 reps.*
Light load. Exhale on the curl, inhale on the return. Rest 90 seconds.

*Seated calf raise — 2 sets × 20 reps.*
Bodyweight or light plate on thighs. Full range of motion — lower the heel below the platform level, rise fully onto the ball of the foot. Rest 60 seconds.

*Dead bug — 2 sets × 8 reps each side.*
Lie on the back, knees bent to 90 degrees, arms pointing to the ceiling. Slowly lower one arm overhead while extending the opposite leg, keeping the lower back pressed gently into the floor. Breathe continuously — exhale as the limbs extend. If the client holds their breath at any point, stop the set. Rest 60 seconds.

**Cool-down (10 minutes)**

Five minutes slow treadmill walk at 2.5 km/h, flat. Five minutes seated stretching: standing hip flexor lunge (30 seconds each side), supine hamstring stretch (30 seconds each side), seated calf stretch (30 seconds each side). Final HR check — below 90 bpm before leaving.

---

### Session 2 — Cardiovascular Conditioning

**Warm-up:** Five minutes recumbent bike at minimal resistance.

**Main work:** 20 minutes on the recumbent bike. HR target 95–108 bpm. RPE 10–11. The client should be able to speak in full sentences throughout. Check HR every 3 minutes and record it. If HR climbs above 108 bpm, reduce resistance immediately.

**Why the recumbent bike in Week 1:** The recumbent position reduces cardiac preload compared to upright exercise and eliminates balance demands, making it the safest cardiovascular starting point for this population.

**Cool-down:** Five minutes at minimal resistance. Five minutes seated rest with HR monitoring.

---

### Session 3 — Upper Body and Core Focus

**Warm-up (10 minutes)**

Five minutes recumbent bike. Then: 10 arm circles each direction, 10 wall slides (arms slide up a wall, elbows bent to 90 degrees, press the arms overhead while keeping the back of the hands and elbows in contact with the wall), 15 band pull-aparts (light resistance band held in both hands at shoulder height, pull the band apart by squeezing the shoulder blades together).

**Working sets**

*Seated cable row (close grip, neutral handles) — 2 sets × 15 reps.*
Sit tall. Initiate the movement by retracting the shoulder blades before bending the elbows. Pull the handles to the lower sternum. Return with control. Exhale on the pull, inhale on the return. Light load. Rest 2 minutes.

*Chest press machine — 2 sets × 15 reps.*
Light load. Exhale on the press. Rest 90 seconds.

*Lat pulldown (wide grip, to chin level) — 2 sets × 15 reps.*
Do not pull behind the neck. Lean back very slightly — approximately 10–15 degrees — and pull the bar to the upper chest. Exhale on the pull-down. Light load. Rest 90 seconds.

*Dumbbell shoulder press (seated) — 2 sets × 12 reps.*
Very light load (3–5 kg). Exhale on the press. Rest 90 seconds.

*Band pull-apart — 2 sets × 15 reps.*
Light band. Arms straight at shoulder height, pull the band apart until the arms are in a T position, squeezing the shoulder blades together. Rest 60 seconds.

*Wall push-up or incline push-up — 2 sets × 10 reps.*
Begin with wall push-ups if the client cannot perform a knee push-up with continuous breathing and controlled tempo. Exhale on the push away from the wall. Rest 90 seconds.

*Dead bug — 2 sets × 8 reps each side.*
As per Session 1. Rest 60 seconds.

**Cool-down (10 minutes)**

Five minutes slow treadmill walk. Five minutes stretching: chest doorway stretch (30 seconds), lat stretch with arm overhead against wall (30 seconds each side), neck side flexion (20 seconds each side — gentle, no overpressure).
